docs.title: Audience
docs.text: This book is written for 10th–12th grade students who are curious about the stories left out of traditional textbooks, willing to take on tedious, hands-on primary- and secondary-source research, and self-motivated. It assumes the civic, geographic, and identity-focused analytical skills built in 9th grade Human Geography and Ethnic Studies (or AP Human Geography), and builds on that foundation with deeper historiography and systemic analysis. Readers should be prepared to examine sensitive topics — race, gender, sexuality, and systemic injustice — with honesty and empathy.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: This file is the seed document used by the learning-graph-generator skill to enumerate concepts, build the dependency graph, and assign concepts to a taxonomy. Keep it focused, concrete, and free of marketing language.

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Absent Narratives: A Comprehensive Study of Marginalized Voices in History

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text: An 18-week (one semester) high school elective asking students to critically consider the impact of race, ethnicity, nationality, gender, and sexuality on the course of human history. Students question, investigate, interpret, and reflect on the stories of those whose life experiences have been marginalized because of these characteristics and identities, and build cultural literacy through self-inquiry and exploration for a more complete understanding of the world and its living history. Hidden history — the untold, overlooked, and intentionally obscured stories of marginalized groups, suppressed events, and alternative perspectives — is studied not for recall of facts alone, but to build global and multicultural relationships, teach empathy across backgrounds, and help every student see their own story reflected in the curriculum. The course fulfills an additional pathway toward Minnesota's ethnic studies course requirement.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school students in grades 10–12 who are curious about the stories left out of traditional textbooks, willing to do tedious hands-on primary- and secondary-source research, and self-motivated. No prior background in historiography is assumed, but students are expected to arrive with the foundational civic, geographic, and identity-focused analytical skills built in 9th grade Human Geography and Ethnic Studies.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• 9th grade Human Geography and Ethnic Studies (or AP Human Geography)
  • Basic civic-literacy skills: reading primary and secondary sources, identifying an author's perspective, comparing accounts of the same event

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
1. What is Hidden History — vocabulary and the study of absent narratives
  2. Historiography — who writes history, whose stories are excluded, and why
  3. Primary and secondary source analysis for uncovering absent narratives
  4. Case study: Manifest Destiny and the narratives it obscured
  5. Government representation: systemic racism and sexism in policy
  6. Gerrymandering and its effects on political representation
  7. Voter intimidation and suppression, historical and contemporary
  8. Economic exclusion: embargoes and their disproportionate impacts
  9. Redlining and housing discrimination
  10. Bias in college admissions
  11. The construction of criminality: what is a criminal, and who decides
  12. Codes, laws, and the justice system's differential treatment of groups
  13. Statistics on prejudice within the justice system
  14. Representation in media: colorism and dominant beauty standards
  15. Bias in news headlines and framing
  16. The social construction of race and its use to justify oppression
  17. Indigenous sovereignty and treaty relationships with the U.S. and Minnesota
  18. Migration, forced displacement, and diaspora
  19. Liberation and civil rights movements, past and present
  20. Language and power: how language has been used for and against marginalized groups

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
To keep the course focused within one semester, the following related topics are intentionally out of scope (some are addressed in the 9th grade Human Geography and Ethnic Studies prerequisite, others belong to other courses):

  • General world-history survey content already covered in prerequisite courses
  • In-depth economic theory beyond the specific case studies of embargoes, redlining, and college admissions
  • Legal training in constitutional or case law beyond what is needed to discuss codes, statutes, and their differential enforcement
  • International comparative government systems outside the U.S./Minnesota context, except where directly relevant to colonialism or migration
  • Clinical or psychological treatments of trauma; the course addresses historical and social analysis, not counseling or therapeutic practice

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
After this course, students will be able to:

  • Remember: Recall key vocabulary of hidden history and historiography; identify major events and case studies (e.g., Manifest Destiny, the U.S. civil rights movement) covered in the course; list the categories of identity (race, ethnicity, nationality, gender, sexuality) central to the course's analytical frame.
  • Understand: Explain why certain narratives have been excluded or minimized from mainstream history; describe how systemic racism, sexism, and other structural forces operate in government, economics, and the justice system; summarize the social construction of race and its historical uses.
  • Apply: Use primary and secondary source analysis methods to investigate an absent narrative of the student's choosing; apply historiographical questions (who wrote this, for whom, and why) to a historical text or media artifact.
  • Analyze: Analyze the role of race, ethnicity, nationality, gender, and sexuality in shaping historical and contemporary events; examine bias in media representation, headlines, and beauty standards; compare how different groups have experienced exclusion from dominant narratives.
  • Evaluate: Evaluate the reliability, perspective, and completeness of historical sources; assess the impact of policies such as redlining, gerrymandering, and voter suppression on marginalized communities; critique how criminality and prejudice are constructed and measured.
  • Create: Research and reconstruct a previously hidden or marginalized historical narrative using primary and secondary sources, presenting it in a way that restores the voice and perspective of the people involved; design an original multimedia or written presentation (e.g., podcast, exhibit, essay, or documentary) that makes an absent narrative accessible to a broader audience; propose a policy or community action that responds to a historical pattern of exclusion identified through the student's own research.

docs.title: Minnesota State Standards Alignment
docs.text:
• 9.1.1.1, 9.1.1.3 — Civic skills; evaluating sources for bias and validity
  • 9.1.6.2 — Trust relationships between Tribal Nations and government
  • 9.3.15.1, 9.3.15.3, 9.3.15.6–9.3.15.8 — Migration, diffusion, sovereignty, colonialism, and political boundaries
  • 9.3.17.1–9.3.17.4 — Identity, sense of place, and the social construction of race
  • 9.5.23.1–9.5.23.6 — Racial/ethnic hierarchies, colorism, language and power
  • 9.5.24.1–9.5.24.2 — Liberation struggles, racial capitalism, Indigenous sovereignty
  • 9.5.25.1–9.5.25.4 — Civil rights movements, contemporary Indigenous representation, the construction of criminality

docs.title: Course Logistics
docs.text:
• Length: One semester (18 weeks)
  • Grade level: 10th–12th
  • Homework load: ~2 hours per week
  • Department: Social Studies (Two Rivers High School)

docs.title: What is this course about?
docs.text: Absent Narratives: A Comprehensive Study of Marginalized Voices in History is an 18-week social studies elective that teaches students to identify, analyze, and help correct the gaps left in traditional historical accounts when the experiences of marginalized groups are minimized or excluded. Rather than simply adding a few new stories to a familiar timeline, the course equips students with an analytical toolkit — concepts like dominant narrative, counter-narrative, historical silence, and marginalization — and then applies that toolkit across fourteen chapters covering historiography, identity, government, economics, the justice system, media, Indigenous sovereignty, migration, civil rights, religion, and language. Case studies such as Manifest Destiny and the Trail of Tears ground abstract concepts in specific historical events. The course culminates in an original capstone research project, where students apply everything they've learned to recover or re-examine an absent narrative of their choosing. Throughout, the emphasis is on evidence-based historical inquiry, not advocacy: students learn to evaluate sources, recognize bias, and build defensible arguments. For a full breakdown of goals, audience, and outcomes, see the course description.

docs.title: Who is this course designed for?
docs.text: This course is built for senior high school students, typically in grades 10 through 12, enrolled in a social studies elective. It assumes a foundational U.S. and world history background comparable to a standard high school sequence, but it does not require prior coursework in sociology, critical theory, or historiography — all specialized vocabulary is introduced and defined as it is used, beginning with Chapter 1 and reinforced throughout the glossary. The course is well suited to students who are curious about how history gets written and whose voices tend to be left out, as well as students preparing for AP-level history, government, or sociology courses that expect comfort with primary-source analysis and argumentative writing. Because the material engages directly with topics like race, gender, sexuality, and systemic injustice, it also works well for students ready to discuss these subjects in an academic, evidence-based setting rather than a purely personal or political one. See the course description for the full audience statement and prerequisite expectations.

docs.title: What prior knowledge or prerequisites do I need before starting?
docs.text: There is no formal prerequisite course, but students should arrive with basic historical literacy: familiarity with major eras of U.S. history (colonization through the twentieth century), the ability to read and summarize a primary source, and comfort writing a structured analytical paragraph. The course does not assume any prior exposure to terms like systemic oppression, intersectionality, or settler colonialism — Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 build this vocabulary from the ground up before it is applied to case studies. Students benefit from basic research skills (using a library database, distinguishing a primary from a secondary source) since these are refined, not introduced, in Chapter 14. The course description lists the full prerequisite expectations, and the glossary can be used to preview key terms before the term begins.

docs.title: How is the course organized?
docs.text: The course is organized into fourteen chapters that build in a deliberate sequence. Chapters 1 through 3 establish the conceptual foundation: historiography and source analysis, the vocabulary of power and exclusion, and the social construction of identity. Chapters 4 through 13 apply that foundation to specific domains — westward expansion, government representation, economic exclusion, the justice system, media, Indigenous sovereignty, migration and colonialism, civil rights movements, religion, and language — each domain building on concepts introduced earlier. Chapter 14 closes the course with research methods and the capstone project, where students design and complete an original investigation. The learning graph shows exactly how each chapter's concepts depend on concepts from earlier chapters, which is useful both for previewing the course and for reviewing before an assessment. The course description provides the full syllabus-level outline.

docs.title: How long does the course take to complete?
docs.text: The course is designed to run across a single 18-week semester, with roughly one chapter covered per week to week and a half, leaving built-in time for the multi-week capstone project in the final chapter. Chapters near the start of the course, which introduce vocabulary and conceptual frameworks, tend to move faster than the applied chapters in the middle of the course, which pair reading with source analysis and discussion. Instructors may compress or extend individual chapters depending on class schedule and depth of discussion desired. See the course description for the recommended pacing guide.

docs.title: How much time should I expect to spend on the course each week?
docs.text: Most weeks require the equivalent of three to five hours of combined class time and independent work: reading the chapter, working through source-analysis exercises, and participating in discussion. Weeks that introduce dense new vocabulary, such as Chapter 2 or Chapter 3, may take longer as students work to internalize new terminology. During the final weeks of the course, when students are researching and producing their capstone project, time commitment increases to reflect independent research, interviews, or archival work. Students should plan their weekly schedule around the course's pacing guide in the course description rather than assuming a flat weekly workload.

docs.title: What is a "counter-narrative" and why does the course center it?
docs.text: A counter-narrative is an account of the past told from the perspective of a group whose experience has been minimized, distorted, or omitted from the dominant narrative — the widely accepted, textbook version of events. The course centers counter-narratives because historical inquiry is incomplete if it only reproduces the perspective of those who held power at the time; a fuller picture requires actively seeking out the accounts that were suppressed, ignored, or never recorded in the first place. Chapter 1 introduces counter-narrative alongside dominant narrative and historical silence as the three core analytical lenses used throughout the rest of the course. For example, the standard account of westward expansion as a story of opportunity and progress is a dominant narrative; the Cherokee, Choctaw, and other nations' accounts of forced removal during the Trail of Tears, examined in Chapter 4, constitute a counter-narrative to that story. Learning to locate, evaluate, and responsibly present counter-narratives is a skill the course returns to in nearly every chapter.

docs.title: How does the course handle sensitive topics like race, gender, and sexuality responsibly?
docs.text: The course treats race, gender, sexuality, and systemic injustice as subjects of rigorous historical and sociological inquiry, not as platforms for personal opinion or political advocacy. Every claim is grounded in documented evidence — primary sources, government records, court cases, scholarly research — and students are taught to distinguish description of a historical mechanism (such as redlining or voter suppression) from editorializing about it. Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 establish precise, shared vocabulary before applying it to charged material, which reduces the chance that discussions rely on vague or inflammatory language. Discussions are structured around evidence and historical mechanism rather than around students' personal identities, and all groups discussed — including religious traditions in Chapter 12 — are treated with equal analytical respect. Teachers are encouraged to set discussion norms at the start of the term. Students who want to preview how a specific topic is framed can consult the relevant chapter directly or the glossary for neutral, precise definitions of contested terms.

docs.title: Do I need to complete the chapters in order?
docs.text: Yes, for the most part. The course is sequenced so that each chapter depends on vocabulary and concepts introduced earlier — for instance, Chapter 5 on voter suppression assumes familiarity with systemic oppression and power structure from Chapter 2. The learning graph documents these dependencies explicitly, and skipping ahead without the prerequisite concepts can make later chapters harder to follow. That said, an instructor may choose to reorder some of the applied chapters (4 through 13) relative to one another once the foundational Chapters 1 through 3 are complete, since many of them draw on the same foundational vocabulary rather than on each other directly. Chapter 14, the capstone, should always come last.

docs.title: What is the capstone project and when do I start working on it?
docs.text: The capstone project is the culminating assignment of the course, introduced and scaffolded in Chapter 14, in which students design and complete an original investigation into an absent narrative of their choosing. Students may present their findings as a documentary, a museum-style exhibit, a policy proposal, or a community action project, applying research methods such as archival research, oral history interviews, and source triangulation covered earlier in the chapter. While the capstone is formally assigned in the final weeks of the course, students are encouraged to start identifying a topic of interest much earlier — many find inspiration in the case studies from Chapters 4 through 13 — so that by the time Chapter 14 begins, they already have a research question in mind rather than starting from a blank page.

docs.title: Where can I find definitions of unfamiliar terms?
docs.text: The glossary contains precise, textbook-style definitions for every key term used across the fourteen chapters, from foundational vocabulary like historical silence and dominant narrative to specific terms like redlining, gerrymandering, and blood quantum. Definitions in the glossary are written to be non-circular and consistent with how the term is used in context, so it is a reliable first stop whenever a chapter introduces language that feels unfamiliar. For a bigger-picture view of how a term relates to other concepts in the course — what it depends on and what depends on it — students can also consult the learning graph, which maps every concept's prerequisites and connections.

docs.title: What is the learning graph and how do I use it to study?
docs.text: The learning graph is a structured map of every concept taught in the course, showing which concepts must be understood before others can make sense — for example, students must understand power structure and systemic oppression before they can fully grasp systemic racism. It is available at learning-graph/index.md. Students can use it in two main ways: prospectively, to preview what background a chapter assumes before diving in, and retrospectively, to review by tracing a concept back through its prerequisites when preparing for an assessment or the capstone project. Concepts that many other concepts depend on — such as power structure, systemic racism, and civil rights movement — sit at high-centrality positions in the graph and are worth mastering early, since a weak grasp of them tends to create confusion several chapters later.

docs.title: What is a power structure?
docs.text: A power structure is the organized arrangement of institutions, laws, and social relationships through which a society distributes authority, resources, and decision-making capacity. Power structures are not necessarily conspiratorial or intentional; they emerge from history, law, custom, and institutional design, and they can persist long after the specific decisions that created them are forgotten. Understanding power structures is foundational to the entire course because nearly every other concept — systemic oppression, marginalization, systemic racism — describes how power structures produce unequal outcomes for different groups. Chapter 2 introduces the concept directly, and it recurs throughout the course: the study of gerrymandering in Chapter 5 and of redlining in Chapter 6 are both examinations of how a power structure operating through law and policy produced durable, measurable inequality. For example, the federal government's establishment of tribal reservations in the nineteenth century created a power structure that still shapes the political and economic status of Indigenous nations today, discussed further in Chapter 9.

docs.title: What is media representation?
docs.text: Media representation refers to how films, television, news, advertising, and other media portray members of particular racial, gender, ethnic, religious, or other social groups — including how frequently they appear, in what roles, and with what degree of nuance or stereotype. Representation matters because media is one of the primary ways people form impressions of groups they have limited direct contact with, so patterns like underrepresentation, tokenized casting, or whitewashing can reinforce the very stereotypes and hierarchies the course examines elsewhere. Chapter 8 is devoted entirely to this concept, covering colorism in media, headline bias, framing effects, and algorithmic bias in what content platforms surface. As a worked example: a 1990s television landscape in which non-white characters appeared primarily in supporting or criminal roles shaped audience assumptions in ways that mirrored — and reinforced — stereotypes examined in Chapter 2. Media representation is a high-centrality concept in the learning graph because it connects to stereotype, framing, propaganda, and counter-storytelling.

docs.title: What is settler colonialism?
docs.text: Settler colonialism is a distinct form of colonialism in which colonizers arrive not merely to extract resources or labor but to permanently replace an Indigenous population and its political, economic, and cultural systems with their own. Unlike extractive colonialism, which can end when the colonizing power withdraws, settler colonialism is structured to be permanent — the settler society itself becomes the new political order. Chapter 4 applies this concept directly to U.S. westward expansion, examining how Manifest Destiny, the Homestead Act, and Indigenous displacement functioned as mechanisms of settler colonialism rather than isolated policy decisions. Chapter 9 and Chapter 10 extend the concept to boarding schools, treaty violations, and comparative global cases. As a worked example, the forced relocation of the Cherokee Nation along the Trail of Tears was not simply a land dispute but part of a broader settler-colonial project to replace Indigenous nations with a U.S. agricultural settler population on their ancestral land.

docs.title: What is systemic racism?
docs.text: Systemic racism describes racial inequality that is produced and reproduced by the ordinary operation of institutions, laws, and policies, rather than by the individual prejudice of any single person. It is distinguished from interpersonal prejudice in that it can persist even when no individual within the system holds racist beliefs, because the rules, defaults, and incentives of the system itself generate unequal outcomes along racial lines. Chapter 2 introduces the concept, and it is examined concretely across the course: Chapter 6 traces systemic racism through redlining and the racial wealth gap, Chapter 7 traces it through sentencing disparity and mass incarceration, and Chapter 5 traces it through voter suppression mechanisms like poll taxes and literacy tests. As a worked example, mid-twentieth-century mortgage lending policies that systematically denied loans in majority-Black neighborhoods produced a measurable, multi-generational wealth gap without requiring every individual loan officer to hold personal racial animus — the discriminatory outcome was built into the system's rules.

docs.title: What is the civil rights movement?
docs.text: The civil rights movement refers to the sustained, organized effort — primarily from the 1950s through the late 1960s in the United States — to dismantle legal segregation, secure voting rights, and achieve equal treatment under the law for Black Americans, though the term is also used more broadly for related movements pursuing legal and social equality for other marginalized groups. Chapter 11 covers the movement in depth, situating it within the longer arc of the legacy of slavery, Reconstruction, and Jim Crow, and examining its core strategies of nonviolent resistance and civil disobedience alongside later desegregation efforts and contemporary activism. The civil rights movement is one of the highest-centrality concepts in the learning graph because so much of the course — voting rights in Chapter 5, the justice system in Chapter 7, and other liberation movements — depends on understanding its strategies, legal victories, and unfinished goals as a reference point.

docs.title: What is language and power?
docs.text: Language and power describes the ways that language — its grammar, vocabulary, accent, and use — both reflects and reinforces social hierarchies, determining whose speech is treated as authoritative, correct, or professional and whose is stigmatized, suppressed, or dismissed. Chapter 13 is devoted to this concept, covering linguistic suppression, dialect bias, naming and identity, and the politics of translation. As a worked example, policies in many nineteenth- and twentieth-century boarding schools that punished Indigenous children for speaking their native languages, discussed in Chapter 9, used language suppression as a direct tool of cultural erasure. Language and power connects to many other concepts in the learning graph, including code-switching, oral tradition, and language revitalization efforts that communities use to reclaim suppressed languages.

docs.title: What is a counter-narrative?
docs.text: A counter-narrative is a historical account that challenges, complicates, or corrects a dominant narrative by centering the experiences and evidence of a group that dominant accounts have minimized or excluded. Counter-narratives are not automatically true simply because they are counter — like any historical claim, they must be supported by evidence — but they are essential because a dominant narrative, by definition, reflects the perspective of whoever held the power to write and preserve the historical record. Chapter 1 introduces the concept, and Chapter 8 extends it into "counter-storytelling" as a media practice. As a worked example, the standard narrative of the American Revolution as a unified colonial fight for liberty is complicated by the counter-narrative of the roughly one-fifth of the colonial population who were enslaved and excluded from the liberty being claimed.

docs.title: What is marginalization?
docs.text: Marginalization is the process by which a group is pushed to the periphery of social, political, or economic life, reducing its members' access to power, resources, and representation relative to the dominant group. Marginalization can occur through explicit exclusion, such as laws denying voting rights, or through more diffuse mechanisms, such as being consistently omitted from historical narratives, media, or public memory. It is one of the ten highest-centrality concepts in the learning graph because it underlies the course's title and its central concern. Chapter 1 introduces marginalization alongside historical silence, and later chapters trace its specific mechanisms: economic marginalization through redlining in Chapter 6, political marginalization through gerrymandering in Chapter 5, and cultural marginalization through media stereotyping in Chapter 8.

docs.title: What is systemic oppression?
docs.text: Systemic oppression is the sustained, structural disadvantage that a group experiences as a result of how laws, institutions, and social norms are organized, as distinct from a single unjust act or an individual's prejudiced attitude. It typically combines multiple mechanisms — legal exclusion, economic disadvantage, cultural marginalization — that reinforce one another over time. Chapter 2 introduces systemic oppression as one of the course's foundational terms, distinguishing it from privilege, power structure, and discrimination. As a worked example, Jim Crow laws combined systemic oppression across multiple domains at once — voting restrictions, segregated and underfunded schools, and employment discrimination — so that no single reform could undo the disadvantage; each domain reinforced the others. This concept underlies most of the applied chapters, from Chapter 5 on government bias to Chapter 7 on the justice system.

docs.title: What is a political boundary?
docs.text: A political boundary is a line — a national border, a state line, a voting district, a reservation boundary — that a governing authority draws to define jurisdiction, and which in turn determines who has access to which rights, resources, and representation. Political boundaries are rarely neutral: their placement often reflects and reinforces existing power structures. Chapter 5 examines political boundaries through gerrymandering, where voting-district lines are drawn to dilute or concentrate a particular group's political power, and Chapter 10 examines border formation as a colonial and postcolonial process that often ignored existing ethnic and national communities. As a worked example, the drawing of reservation boundaries in the nineteenth century, discussed in Chapter 9, repeatedly redefined the land available to tribal nations, directly shaping the scope of their sovereignty.

docs.title: What is a dominant narrative?
docs.text: A dominant narrative is the version of a historical event or period that becomes widely accepted, taught, and repeated — typically because it reflects the perspective, interests, or records of the group that held political, economic, or cultural power at the time. Dominant narratives are not necessarily fabricated; they are often accurate as far as they go, but they are incomplete, omitting or minimizing perspectives that complicate the story. Chapter 1 introduces dominant narrative directly alongside counter-narrative and historical silence as one of the course's three foundational analytical lenses. As a worked example, the "frontier myth" examined in Chapter 4 — the dominant narrative of westward expansion as heroic settlement of "empty" land — omits the fact that the land was inhabited, governed, and actively defended by Indigenous nations.

docs.title: What is historical silence?
docs.text: Historical silence refers to the absence or suppression of a group's experience within the historical record — not because nothing happened, but because the events were not documented, the documentation was destroyed or ignored, or the people involved lacked the power to have their account preserved. Historical silence differs from simple gaps in evidence caused by the passage of time: it specifically describes silences that are patterned along lines of power, race, gender, or class. Chapter 1 introduces the concept as a companion to dominant narrative and counter-narrative. As a worked example, the perspectives of enslaved people are historically silent in most plantation records, which were written by enslavers; scholars have had to turn to oral histories, slave narratives, and archaeological evidence to partially recover these silenced voices, a method explored further in Chapter 14.

docs.title: What is intersectionality?
docs.text: Intersectionality is the framework for understanding how a person's overlapping social identities — such as race, gender, class, and sexuality — combine to produce experiences of privilege or disadvantage that cannot be understood by examining any single identity category alone. Chapter 3 introduces intersectionality as part of the course's study of identity formation, alongside race, gender, sexuality, classism, and ableism. As a worked example, a Black woman's experience of workplace discrimination may differ from that of a Black man or a white woman, because the intersection of race and gender produces a distinct set of barriers not fully captured by studying race or gender in isolation — this is explored further in Chapter 11 through the experience of Black women within the suffrage and civil rights movements. Intersectionality is a widely used analytical tool across the social sciences, not a claim about anyone's worth or identity.

docs.title: What is social construction?
docs.text: Social construction refers to the idea that certain categories people often treat as fixed or natural — such as race, gender, or criminality — are in fact created and given meaning by societies through history, law, and custom, and can therefore vary across time and place. Describing something as socially constructed does not mean it has no real effects; socially constructed categories like race have had profound, measurable consequences precisely because societies have organized laws and institutions around them. Chapter 3 introduces the concept directly, and Chapter 7 extends it to the idea of criminality as a social construction shaped by selective enforcement. As a worked example, racial categories used in the nineteenth-century United States census changed multiple times, reflecting shifting social and legal definitions of race rather than any biological change in the population.

docs.title: What is privilege?
docs.text: Privilege refers to unearned social, economic, or institutional advantages that a person receives as a result of belonging to a particular group, independent of individual merit or effort. Privilege is the structural complement to systemic oppression: where oppression describes disadvantage imposed on a group, privilege describes the corresponding advantage enjoyed, often invisibly, by another group within the same power structure. Chapter 2 introduces privilege alongside power structure and systemic oppression as foundational vocabulary for the course. As a worked example, legacy admissions policies at universities, examined in Chapter 6, extend an advantage to applicants whose relatives previously attended the institution — a group that, for historical reasons tied to past exclusion, is disproportionately white and wealthy.

docs.title: What is a stereotype?
docs.text: A stereotype is an oversimplified, widely shared belief about the characteristics of a group, applied to individual members of that group regardless of their actual traits. Stereotypes can be positive-seeming on the surface but are still reductive, and they function as a mechanism through which prejudice and discrimination are formed and justified. Chapter 2 introduces stereotype alongside prejudice, discrimination, and bias as related but distinct concepts. Chapter 8 examines how media repetition of stereotypes — such as tokenized casting or narrow role assignment — reinforces them in the broader culture. As a worked example, the persistent portrayal of a single ethnic group as either uniformly criminal or uniformly "model" citizens in twentieth-century film are both stereotypes, even though one sounds complimentary, because both flatten a diverse population into a single trait.

docs.title: What is erasure?
docs.text: Erasure is the process by which a group's presence, contributions, or perspective are removed or omitted from historical accounts, cultural memory, or public representation, whether through deliberate suppression or the accumulated effect of who gets to record and preserve history. Erasure is closely related to historical silence but emphasizes the active or ongoing removal of a narrative that was once present, rather than its original absence from the record. Chapter 2 introduces erasure as part of the course's vocabulary of exclusion, and Chapter 4 applies it directly to the erasure of Indigenous voices from the dominant narrative of westward expansion. Language erasure is also examined in Chapter 13, where the suppression of Indigenous languages in boarding schools functioned as a tool of broader cultural erasure.

docs.title: What is tokenism?
docs.text: Tokenism is the practice of including a small, symbolic number of individuals from a marginalized group — in a workplace, a media production, or an institution — in order to project an appearance of diversity or inclusion without addressing the underlying structural barriers that limit broader representation. Chapter 2 introduces tokenism alongside representation and inclusion. Chapter 8 examines "tokenized casting" specifically, where a media production includes a single character from an underrepresented group, often in a limited or stereotyped role, while the broader cast and creative team remain unchanged. As a worked example, a film industry that includes exactly one prominent character of a given background per project, without changing who writes, directs, or produces, is engaging in tokenism rather than substantive representation.

docs.title: What is representation, and how does it differ from inclusion?
docs.text: Representation refers to the presence and portrayal of a group within a given space — media, government, curricula, institutions — while inclusion refers to the deeper degree to which that group's members have genuine voice, decision-making power, and belonging within that space, not just numerical presence. A group can be represented without being included, as tokenism demonstrates: a single visible member of a group does not guarantee that group's perspective shapes decisions. Chapter 2 introduces both terms together, and Chapter 8 applies representation specifically to media, examining both how frequently groups appear and how meaningfully their stories are told. Political representation is examined in Chapter 5, where gerrymandering can technically preserve a district's demographic makeup while diluting its actual political voice.

docs.title: What is the difference between equity and equality?
docs.text: Equality means giving every individual or group the same resources or treatment, regardless of their starting position, while equity means distributing resources or support based on each individual or group's specific needs and circumstances, with the goal of reaching a comparable outcome. Chapter 2 introduces both terms as foundational vocabulary, distinguishing them precisely so the terms are not used interchangeably later in the course. As a worked example, providing every school district with an identical per-student budget is equality, but because some districts inherited far less property-tax wealth as a result of historical redlining (examined in Chapter 6), an equal budget may not produce equal educational outcomes — an equity-based approach would allocate additional resources to historically under-resourced districts to help close that gap.

docs.title: What is a racial hierarchy?
docs.text: A racial hierarchy is a socially constructed ranking of racial groups, embedded in laws, institutions, and cultural attitudes, that assigns different levels of status, opportunity, and treatment to different groups. Racial hierarchies are not natural or biological; they are constructed and maintained through specific historical mechanisms — legal classification, immigration policy, segregation — that the course examines in detail. Chapter 3 introduces racial hierarchy alongside colorism and beauty standards, both of which often reflect and reinforce a racial hierarchy within and across groups. As a worked example, colonial-era legal codes that assigned different rights to different racial categories, discussed further in Chapter 10, explicitly constructed a racial hierarchy that shaped inheritance, labor, and citizenship for generations.

docs.title: What is cultural identity?
docs.text: Cultural identity is the sense of belonging a person derives from shared language, traditions, religion, history, or community, which contributes to how individuals understand themselves and are understood by others. Cultural identity can be a source of resilience and continuity, particularly for communities whose cultural identity has been targeted for suppression. Chapter 3 introduces cultural identity as one component of identity formation, alongside race, ethnicity, and nationality. Chapter 9 and Chapter 13 examine cultural identity under threat, from the boarding school era's attempts at cultural suppression to ongoing language revitalization efforts that communities use to reclaim and strengthen cultural identity across generations.

docs.title: What is colonialism?
docs.text: Colonialism is the practice by which one country or power establishes control over another territory and its people, typically to extract resources, labor, or strategic advantage, governing the territory through political, economic, or military domination. Chapter 10 introduces colonialism as part of the course's global and comparative perspective, alongside imperialism, forced migration, and diaspora. Colonialism is distinguished from its specific variant, settler colonialism, examined in Chapter 4, in which the colonizing population intends to permanently replace, rather than simply govern or extract from, the existing population. As a worked example, European colonial administration in parts of Africa and Asia, which governed through local intermediaries to extract resources without large-scale permanent settlement, illustrates colonialism without the settler-replacement dynamic of settler colonialism.

docs.title: What is forced migration and diaspora?
docs.text: Forced migration is the involuntary displacement of people from their homeland due to conflict, persecution, environmental catastrophe, or economic coercion, while diaspora refers to the resulting dispersed community that maintains cultural, religious, or emotional ties to its place of origin even while living elsewhere, often across multiple generations. Chapter 10 covers both concepts together, alongside displacement, immigration policy, and the refugee experience. As a worked example, the transatlantic slave trade produced one of history's largest forced migrations, and the resulting African diaspora across the Americas retained, adapted, and transformed cultural and religious practices — a pattern examined further in Chapter 12 through the study of African diasporic religion.

docs.title: What is Indigenous sovereignty?
docs.text: Indigenous sovereignty is the inherent authority of Indigenous nations to govern themselves, their land, and their people, independent of but often in complex legal relationship with the surrounding nation-state. In the United States, tribal nations hold a distinct legal status recognized through treaties and federal law, giving them authority over many internal matters even while operating within the broader framework of U.S. federal authority. Chapter 9 is devoted to this concept, examining treaty rights, federal recognition, self-determination, and Minnesota Tribal Nations as a regional case study. As a worked example, a tribal nation's authority to operate its own court system, set its own membership criteria, and regulate certain economic activity on its land reflects the exercise of Indigenous sovereignty, even as the boundaries of that sovereignty have been repeatedly contested and narrowed through U.S. policy, as discussed in Chapter 4.

docs.title: What is cultural diffusion, and why does it matter to marginalized histories?
docs.text: Cultural diffusion refers to the spread of ideas, customs, technologies, languages, and artistic forms from one society or group to another through contact, trade, migration, or conquest. Historians studying marginalized voices pay close attention to cultural diffusion because dominant historical narratives often erase the contributions that colonized, enslaved, or migrant populations made to the cultures that absorbed or displaced them. A well-known example is the Columbian Exchange following 1492, when crops, livestock, diseases, and cultural practices moved between the Americas, Europe, and Africa. While textbooks frequently frame this exchange as a story of European innovation, a more complete account recognizes that Indigenous agricultural knowledge (such as maize, potato, and cacao cultivation) reshaped global diets and economies, and that enslaved Africans carried rice-cultivation techniques, culinary traditions, and musical forms that fundamentally shaped the culture of the Americas. Studying cultural diffusion critically means asking who is credited as the originator of an idea or practice, whose labor enabled its spread, and whose voice is missing from the traditional account. This concept is closely tied to the textbook's broader goal of recovering absent narratives, since diffusion is rarely a neutral or symmetrical process; it is often entangled with unequal power relationships. See chapters/10-migration-colonialism-and-global-perspectives/index.md for a full treatment of how diffusion intersects with migration and colonialism.

docs.title: How does source bias affect the reliability of a historical account?
docs.text: Source bias occurs when the perspective, motives, social position, or limitations of the person or institution creating a historical record shape what is included, omitted, or emphasized. Every historical source, whether a government document, newspaper article, diary, or photograph, was produced by someone with a particular vantage point, and that vantage point inevitably influences the content. Recognizing source bias does not mean dismissing a source as useless; rather, it means reading the source critically, asking who created it, for what purpose, for what audience, and what the creator stood to gain or lose by presenting events a certain way. For example, a plantation owner's ledger might record enslaved people only as property with monetary value, while an abolitionist newspaper covering the same plantation might emphasize testimonies of abuse; neither source alone gives a complete picture, but together, and read against their respective biases, they can reveal a fuller truth. Historians address source bias by triangulating multiple sources, seeking out perspectives from marginalized groups themselves when they exist, and explicitly naming the gaps left by biased or missing records. This textbook returns repeatedly to source bias because absent narratives frequently exist precisely because the dominant sources of a given era silenced or ignored them. Chapters/01-foundations-of-historical-inquiry/index.md introduces the analytical tools students need to identify and account for source bias in primary and secondary materials.

docs.title: What does narrative reconstruction mean in historical research?
docs.text: Narrative reconstruction is the scholarly process of assembling a coherent historical account from fragmentary, biased, or incomplete evidence, particularly when the subjects of that history were denied the opportunity to record their own experiences. Because marginalized groups were often excluded from formal record-keeping, denied literacy, or had their testimonies suppressed or destroyed, historians must reconstruct their experiences indirectly, using court records, oral histories collected generations later, material culture, demographic data, and careful cross-referencing of documents produced by others. A well-known instance of narrative reconstruction is the Federal Writers' Project of the 1930s, which collected interviews with formerly enslaved people; although the interviews are invaluable, historians must also account for the fact that many interviewers were white and interviewees may have shaped their answers accordingly, decades after emancipation. Effective narrative reconstruction requires transparency about method: researchers must state explicitly which claims are directly evidenced, which are inferred, and which remain uncertain. This textbook's capstone research project asks students to practice narrative reconstruction themselves, working with limited or biased source material to build a defensible historical account of an underrepresented person, community, or event. See chapters/14-research-methods-and-capstone-project/index.md for the step-by-step methodology used in the capstone assignment.

docs.title: Why is author perspective an essential factor in evaluating a text?
docs.text: Author perspective refers to the combination of a writer's identity, social position, historical moment, and personal or institutional interests that shape how they interpret and present information. No historical text is written from a neutral, view-from-nowhere standpoint; every author selects which facts to include, how to frame events, and which voices to quote or paraphrase. Understanding author perspective allows students to distinguish between what happened and how a particular writer chose to represent what happened. For instance, a 19th-century newspaper editorial and a private letter written by a participant in the same event may describe it in strikingly different terms because the editorial writer served a public, often politically motivated, audience, while the letter writer had no such constraint. Evaluating author perspective involves researching the author's background, social status, likely audience, and the broader political or cultural pressures of their era. It also requires comparing an author's account against other sources to identify where perspective has shaped, exaggerated, or omitted details. This skill is foundational to the entire textbook, since recovering absent narratives depends on recognizing whose perspective dominated the historical record and whose was excluded. Chapters/01-foundations-of-historical-inquiry/index.md develops this skill through guided primary-source analysis exercises.

docs.title: What role does critical thinking play in the study of history?
docs.text: Critical thinking in historical study is the disciplined practice of questioning sources, evaluating evidence, identifying assumptions, and resisting the temptation to accept a single narrative as complete or objective. Rather than passively absorbing information, a critical thinker asks who produced a claim, what evidence supports it, what alternative explanations exist, and whose interests are served by a particular version of events. In the context of marginalized histories, critical thinking is essential because the dominant narrative taught in many textbooks has often been shaped by the perspectives of those who held political, economic, or social power, while the experiences of excluded groups were minimized or omitted. A critical thinker examines gaps and silences in the record as evidence in themselves, asking not only what a source says but what it conspicuously does not say. Critical thinking also requires distinguishing between correlation and causation, recognizing logical fallacies, and being willing to revise a prior conclusion when new evidence emerges. This textbook is structured to build critical thinking incrementally, moving from basic source evaluation in the opening chapter to complex, multi-source argumentation in the capstone project. Chapters/01-foundations-of-historical-inquiry/index.md introduces the core critical thinking framework that recurs throughout every subsequent chapter.

docs.title: What is meant by "hidden history," and how do historians uncover it?
docs.text: Hidden history refers to events, individuals, movements, and social conditions that were deliberately suppressed, casually omitted, or structurally excluded from mainstream historical narratives, often because the people involved lacked the political power or institutional access to ensure their experiences were recorded and preserved. Hidden history is not necessarily secret in the sense of being actively concealed by conspiracy; more often it results from unequal access to publishing, education, and archives, combined with the biases of those who decided what counted as historically significant. A notable example is the story of the "Six Triple Eight," the only all-Black, all-female Women's Army Corps unit deployed overseas during World War II, whose critical mail-sorting work went largely unrecognized in official military histories for decades until later research and advocacy brought it to public attention. Historians uncover hidden history through archival research in overlooked collections, oral history projects, demographic and economic data analysis, and cross-referencing marginal references in otherwise mainstream documents. Recovering hidden history requires patience, since the very absence of easily accessible sources is often the central obstacle. This textbook's title, Absent Narratives, directly reflects this concept, and chapters/01-foundations-of-historical-inquiry/index.md provides the methodological starting point for identifying and researching hidden histories throughout the following chapters.

docs.title: Why must historical events be understood within their historical context?
docs.text: Historical context refers to the political, economic, social, and cultural circumstances surrounding an event, without which the event's meaning and significance cannot be accurately understood. Judging past actions, statements, or policies solely by present-day standards, a practice sometimes called presentism, risks distorting historical understanding by ignoring the constraints, assumptions, and available options that shaped decisions at the time. At the same time, providing context is not the same as excusing harmful actions; understanding why a discriminatory law was passed in a given era, for example, helps explain its persistence and consequences without minimizing the harm it caused. Establishing historical context requires researching contemporaneous economic conditions, prevailing legal frameworks, dominant ideologies, and the range of viewpoints that existed at the time, including dissenting or marginalized ones that may not have been widely publicized. This textbook consistently pairs each case study with background on the surrounding decade's political climate, economic pressures, and social attitudes so that students can evaluate primary sources accurately rather than anachronistically. Chapters/01-foundations-of-historical-inquiry/index.md establishes the practice of contextual analysis that is applied to every subsequent case study in the book, from Manifest Destiny to twentieth-century civil rights movements.

docs.title: What defines a liberation struggle, and how do these movements typically unfold?
docs.text: A liberation struggle is an organized, sustained effort by a group facing systemic oppression, such as enslavement, colonization, segregation, or disenfranchisement, to secure freedom, legal equality, or self-determination. Liberation struggles typically combine multiple strategies, including legal challenges, direct action, civil disobedience, armed resistance in some cases, and cultural or artistic expression that builds group identity and public sympathy. A widely studied example is the Montgomery Bus Boycott of 1955 to 1956, in which the Black community of Montgomery, Alabama, sustained a thirteen-month boycott of the city's segregated bus system following Rosa Parks's arrest, combining economic pressure, grassroots coordination, and a successful legal challenge that reached the Supreme Court. Liberation struggles are rarely spontaneous; they typically build on years of prior organizing, mutual aid networks, and smaller acts of resistance that historians must trace to understand how a movement reached a decisive moment. These struggles also often involve internal debate over strategy and goals, and historical accounts that flatten a movement into a single leader or a single tactic tend to obscure the collective labor that sustained it. This textbook examines liberation struggles as case studies in organized resistance to systemic injustice. Chapters/11-civil-rights-and-liberation-movements/index.md covers the strategies, leadership structures, and outcomes of major liberation movements in depth.

docs.title: What is redlining?
docs.text: Redlining was the practice, formalized by federal housing agencies in the 1930s, of color-coding maps to rate neighborhoods for mortgage lending risk, with neighborhoods that had significant Black or immigrant populations typically outlined in red and marked as too risky for loans, regardless of the actual financial reliability of residents. Because homeownership has historically been the primary way American families build intergenerational wealth, redlining directly produced the racial wealth gap examined in Chapter 6. As a worked example, two families with identical incomes in 1950 — one in a "greenlined" white neighborhood and one in a redlined Black neighborhood — would have had dramatically different access to mortgage credit, meaning only one could build home equity to pass to the next generation, a gap that compounds over decades even after redlining was formally outlawed in 1968.

docs.title: What is gerrymandering?
docs.text: Gerrymandering is the practice of drawing electoral district boundaries to give one political party, or one racial or demographic group, a disproportionate advantage or disadvantage in elections, either by concentrating opposing voters into as few districts as possible ("packing") or spreading them thinly across many districts so they cannot form a majority anywhere ("cracking"). Chapter 5 examines gerrymandering as a mechanism of systemic bias in government representation, alongside voter suppression and political boundary manipulation more broadly. As a worked example, splitting a cohesive minority-majority neighborhood across four different districts, each of which remains majority non-minority overall, can legally dilute that community's collective voting power without denying any individual the right to vote.

docs.title: What is sentencing disparity?
docs.text: Sentencing disparity refers to documented differences in the length or severity of criminal sentences handed down to people who committed comparable offenses, correlated with factors such as race, income, or geography rather than solely with the facts of the crime. Chapter 7 examines sentencing disparity as one of several mechanisms, alongside selective enforcement and implicit bias, through which the justice system produces unequal outcomes. As a worked example, federal sentencing guidelines that historically punished crack cocaine offenses — more common in poorer, disproportionately Black communities — far more severely than pharmacologically similar powder cocaine offenses produced measurable, well-documented sentencing disparities that contributed to mass incarceration along racial lines.

docs.title: What is colorism?
docs.text: Colorism is a form of discrimination based on skin tone, in which lighter-skinned individuals — often within the same racial or ethnic group — receive social, economic, or cultural advantages that darker-skinned individuals do not. Colorism can operate independently of racism and can occur within a community as well as between communities, and it is frequently reinforced by beauty standards. Chapter 3 introduces colorism alongside racial hierarchy and beauty standard, and Chapter 8 traces colorism in media, noting how lighter-skinned actors are frequently cast more often and in more favorable roles than darker-skinned actors of the same background.

docs.title: What is a poll tax?
docs.text: A poll tax was a fee historically required to be paid before a citizen could vote, used in many Southern U.S. states after Reconstruction specifically to disenfranchise Black voters and poor white voters who could not afford the fee. Poll taxes were one of several mechanisms, alongside literacy tests, used to circumvent the Fifteenth Amendment's guarantee of voting rights regardless of race. Chapter 5 examines the poll tax as part of its study of voter suppression, noting that poll taxes were not formally banned in federal elections until the Twenty-Fourth Amendment in 1964 and in state elections until a 1966 Supreme Court ruling.

docs.title: What is a literacy test, in the context of voting rights?
docs.text: A literacy test, in this context, was a legally required demonstration of reading or comprehension ability that Southern states used after Reconstruction to disqualify Black voters from registering, often through deliberately subjective or impossibly difficult questions administered unevenly — white applicants frequently passed regardless of actual literacy, while Black applicants were failed regardless of their qualifications. Chapter 5 examines literacy tests alongside poll taxes as twin mechanisms of voter suppression that persisted for nearly a century after the Fifteenth Amendment nominally guaranteed the right to vote.

docs.title: What was the Voting Rights Act?
docs.text: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 was landmark federal legislation that outlawed literacy tests, poll taxes, and other discriminatory voting practices, and required jurisdictions with a history of voting discrimination to obtain federal approval before changing their voting laws. It was one of the most significant legislative achievements of the civil rights movement, examined in Chapter 11, and its protections are discussed in Chapter 5 alongside later legal developments, including a 2013 Supreme Court decision that weakened its preclearance requirement, which subsequent chapters connect to renewed concerns about gerrymandering and voter suppression.

docs.title: What are legacy admissions?
docs.text: Legacy admissions is a college admissions practice that gives preferential consideration to applicants who have a parent, grandparent, or other relative who previously attended the same institution. Chapter 6 examines legacy admissions as a form of economic and racial exclusion, because the practice extends an advantage to applicants whose families were already admitted in earlier generations — generations during which many selective universities either formally excluded or severely limited admission of Black, Jewish, and other minority students. As a worked example, a university that has admitted an overwhelmingly white student body for most of its history will, through legacy admissions, continue extending an admissions advantage disproportionately to white applicants today, even with no explicit racial criterion in the current policy.

docs.title: What are reparations?
docs.text: Reparations refers to proposed or enacted measures — financial payment, land restitution, formal apology, or targeted policy investment — intended to compensate a group for historical injustices committed against it or its ancestors, such as slavery or Indigenous land seizure. Chapter 6 examines reparations proposals in the context of the racial wealth gap produced by slavery, Jim Crow, and redlining, presenting the range of historical and contemporary reparations proposals as a subject of ongoing public debate grounded in documented economic harm, rather than advocating for any specific policy outcome.

docs.title: What is gentrification?
docs.text: Gentrification is the process by which a historically lower-income, often minority, urban neighborhood undergoes an influx of wealthier residents and investment, typically resulting in rising property values and rents that can displace long-term residents who can no longer afford to remain. Chapter 6 examines gentrification alongside redlining and housing discrimination as related but distinct mechanisms shaping who has access to housing and neighborhood investment. As a worked example, a neighborhood that was denied mortgage investment for decades under redlining, and later experiences a wave of new investment and rising rents once outside developers recognize its low property values, illustrates how the same neighborhood can be shaped by exclusionary and then displacing economic forces within a single generation.

docs.title: What is racial profiling?
docs.text: Racial profiling is the practice of law enforcement targeting individuals for suspicion, stops, or searches based primarily on their race or ethnicity rather than on individualized evidence of wrongdoing. Chapter 7 examines racial profiling as a manifestation of implicit bias operating within policing, connecting it to selective enforcement and the broader construction of criminality discussed earlier in the chapter. Racial profiling is documented through statistical analysis of stop, search, and arrest rates that show significant racial disparities even when controlling for underlying crime rates in a given area.

docs.title: What is the school-to-prison pipeline?
docs.text: The school-to-prison pipeline describes the pattern by which harsh school discipline policies — suspension, expulsion, and referral to law enforcement for behavior once handled internally — disproportionately push students, especially Black and Latino students and students with disabilities, out of the classroom and into the juvenile and adult criminal justice systems. Chapter 7 examines the school-to-prison pipeline alongside restorative justice, which is often proposed as an alternative disciplinary approach that keeps students in school while still addressing misconduct.

docs.title: What is whitewashing in media?
docs.text: Whitewashing in media is the practice of casting white actors in roles originally written for, or historically based on, people of color, or of altering a story's characters to be white in adaptation. Chapter 8 examines whitewashing alongside tokenized casting as two related but distinct patterns of media misrepresentation — one involving the wholesale replacement of a character's identity, the other involving limited and often stereotyped inclusion. As a worked example, historical films that cast white actors to portray real, documented people of color from history is a well-studied instance of whitewashing.

docs.title: What is algorithmic bias?
docs.text: Algorithmic bias refers to systematic and unfair skew in the outputs of automated systems — search engines, recommendation systems, content moderation tools, facial recognition software — that results in different treatment or outcomes for different demographic groups, often because the data used to train the system reflected existing social biases. Chapter 8 examines algorithmic bias as a contemporary extension of media representation, since the algorithms that determine which content, images, or news stories a person sees can reproduce stereotypes and underrepresentation at a scale no individual editor could match.

docs.title: What is blood quantum?
docs.text: Blood quantum is a system, historically imposed by the U.S. federal government, that measures an individual's Indigenous ancestry as a fraction in order to determine eligibility for tribal enrollment, federal recognition, or associated benefits. Chapter 9 examines blood quantum as a contested legacy of federal policy, noting that many tribal nations today set their own membership criteria — which may or may not rely on blood quantum — as an exercise of self-determination, since the concept originated as an externally imposed classification rather than an Indigenous one.

docs.title: What was the boarding school era?
docs.text: The boarding school era refers to the period, roughly from the late nineteenth through much of the twentieth century, during which the U.S. government and religious institutions operated schools designed to forcibly assimilate Indigenous children by separating them from their families, punishing them for speaking their native languages or practicing their traditions, and often subjecting them to abuse. Chapter 9 examines the boarding school era as a central mechanism of cultural suppression, connecting it to the language suppression discussed in Chapter 13 and to ongoing repatriation and healing efforts.

docs.title: What is code-switching?
docs.text: Code-switching is the practice of alternating between two or more languages, dialects, or registers of speech depending on social context, often used by speakers of a stigmatized dialect to navigate settings — school, work, media — where a different dialect is treated as standard or professional. Chapter 13 examines code-switching as both a practical survival skill and a reflection of dialect bias, since the need to code-switch typically falls on speakers of non-dominant dialects rather than on speakers of the dialect treated as the default.

docs.title: What is dialect bias?
docs.text: Dialect bias is the tendency to judge speakers of a non-standard or regional dialect as less intelligent, less educated, or less professional than speakers of a dialect treated as the linguistic default, even though linguists consider all dialects equally structured and rule-governed. Chapter 13 examines dialect bias as a concrete mechanism of language and power, connecting it to code-switching and to naming and identity as related ways that language use is policed along social lines.

docs.title: What was the Trail of Tears?
docs.text: The Trail of Tears refers to the forced removal, beginning in the 1830s, of the Cherokee Nation and other southeastern Indigenous nations from their ancestral homelands to designated territory west of the Mississippi River, a journey during which thousands died from exposure, disease, and starvation. Chapter 4 presents the Trail of Tears as a central case study in the mechanisms of Indigenous displacement carried out under the ideology of Manifest Destiny, and connects it to the broader pattern of treaty violation examined in Chapter 9.

docs.title: What are treaty rights?
docs.text: Treaty rights are the specific legal rights and protections — often including hunting, fishing, land use, or self-governance provisions — that the U.S. federal government formally agreed to in treaties with Indigenous nations, agreements that carry the force of federal law even when they have been violated or ignored in practice. Chapter 9 examines treaty rights as a foundation of Indigenous sovereignty, noting that many treaty rights remain legally enforceable today and are periodically reaffirmed through litigation, even after more than a century of federal policy that sought to diminish them.

docs.title: What is systemic sexism, and how does it differ from individual acts of discrimination?
docs.text: Systemic sexism refers to patterns of gender-based disadvantage that are embedded in laws, institutional policies, economic structures, and cultural norms, rather than isolated instances of individual prejudice. While an individual act of discrimination involves one person treating another unfairly because of their gender, systemic sexism operates through structures that produce unequal outcomes even when no single actor intends harm, such as hiring practices, wage-setting formulas, property laws, or voting eligibility rules that historically excluded women or disadvantaged them by default. Identifying systemic sexism requires examining aggregate data, such as wage gaps, representation in government and leadership positions, and legal exclusions that persisted across generations, rather than relying solely on individual testimony. Because systemic sexism is embedded in institutions, it often persists after individual attitudes change, since laws, organizational cultures, and economic structures can take much longer to reform than public opinion. This textbook examines systemic sexism as it intersects with political representation and government policy, tracing how formal legal barriers such as restricted suffrage and property rights created disadvantages that outlasted their formal repeal. Chapters/05-government-representation-and-systemic-bias/index.md analyzes the specific legal and institutional mechanisms through which systemic sexism has shaped government representation in the United States.

docs.title: What is civic participation, and what barriers have historically limited it?
docs.text: Civic participation encompasses the range of activities through which individuals engage with public life and governance, including voting, attending public meetings, serving on juries, running for office, petitioning government, and organizing or joining advocacy groups. Throughout American history, formal and informal barriers have restricted civic participation for specific groups, including property requirements, poll taxes, literacy tests, citizenship restrictions, and social intimidation that discouraged participation even where legal barriers had been removed. Studying the history of civic participation requires distinguishing between formal legal rights, such as the extension of suffrage, and the practical ability to exercise those rights, since legal enfranchisement did not always translate into equal access at the ballot box or in public office. Historians also examine informal civic participation, such as community organizing, mutual aid societies, and petition campaigns, which allowed excluded groups to exert political influence even when formal channels were closed to them. Understanding the uneven history of civic participation helps explain persistent disparities in political representation that continue to shape government policy today. Chapters/05-government-representation-and-systemic-bias/index.md traces how barriers to civic participation were constructed, enforced, and gradually challenged across different periods of American history.

docs.title: What is political persuasion, and what techniques have historically been used to shape public opinion?
docs.text: Political persuasion refers to the deliberate use of rhetoric, imagery, media, and argumentation to influence public attitudes toward a policy, candidate, or ideology. Historical actors have employed a range of persuasion techniques, including appeals to fear, patriotism, economic self-interest, and moral authority, often disseminated through newspapers, pamphlets, political cartoons, speeches, and, in the twentieth century, radio, film, and television. Studying political persuasion historically requires analyzing not just the content of a persuasive message but its intended audience, the media through which it was distributed, and the social or economic conditions that made the audience receptive or resistant to it. Propaganda represents an extreme and often government-sponsored form of political persuasion designed to shape mass opinion, sometimes through selective or misleading information. Understanding the history of political persuasion is essential to interpreting primary sources critically, since campaign materials, editorials, and public speeches were rarely neutral accounts of events but were instead crafted to achieve specific political outcomes. This concept connects directly to the textbook's broader emphasis on source bias and author perspective. Chapters/05-government-representation-and-systemic-bias/index.md examines specific historical campaigns of political persuasion and their effects on public policy and representation.

docs.title: What factors have historically shaped public trust in government?
docs.text: Government trust refers to the degree of confidence that citizens place in public institutions to act competently, fairly, and in the public interest. Historically, trust in government has fluctuated in response to specific events, including wars, economic crises, corruption scandals, and documented instances of government mistreatment of specific populations. For marginalized communities, government trust has often been shaped by direct experience with discriminatory policies, such as segregation laws, unequal enforcement of civil rights protections, or documented abuses like unethical medical experimentation conducted without informed consent. Historians studying government trust examine public opinion data where available, but also rely on community records, journalism, and testimony to understand how trust or distrust developed differently across different populations within the same country and time period. Declining trust in government among a particular group is rarely irrational; it typically reflects a documented pattern of broken promises, unequal treatment, or exclusion from decision-making processes. Understanding the historical roots of government trust and distrust helps explain contemporary patterns of political engagement and skepticism. Chapters/05-government-representation-and-systemic-bias/index.md explores how specific government actions and policies built or eroded trust among different communities over time.

docs.title: How do codes and laws function as tools of both order and exclusion?
docs.text: Codes and laws are the formal rules established by governing authorities to regulate behavior, and throughout history they have served dual functions: maintaining social order and, in many documented cases, formalizing the exclusion or control of specific populations. Historical examples include slave codes, which regulated and restricted the lives of enslaved people, and Black codes enacted after the Civil War, which restricted the freedoms of newly emancipated African Americans through vagrancy laws, labor contracts, and restricted property rights. Studying codes and laws requires close textual analysis of statutory language, examination of how laws were enforced in practice, which sometimes differed significantly from their written text, and research into who drafted the laws and whose interests they served. Historians also examine how affected communities responded to restrictive codes, whether through legal challenges, migration, covert resistance, or organized political action to repeal unjust statutes. Because laws carry the authority of the state, they leave relatively well-documented paper trails compared to informal social practices, making legal history one of the more accessible ways to trace the formal architecture of discrimination over time. Chapters/07-justice-system-and-criminality/index.md examines how specific codes and laws shaped the justice system's treatment of marginalized populations.

docs.title: What is the framing effect, and how does it influence historical media coverage?
docs.text: The framing effect describes how the presentation, emphasis, and word choice used to describe an event or issue shapes audience perception and judgment, independent of the underlying facts. In media coverage, framing determines which details are highlighted, which are omitted, what headline is chosen, and what visual imagery accompanies a story, all of which influence how readers interpret events. Historical newspaper coverage of labor strikes, protests, and civil rights demonstrations often illustrates the framing effect clearly: the same event could be described as a "riot" or a "protest," a "mob" or a "movement," depending on the publication's editorial stance and audience. These framing choices had real consequences, shaping public sympathy, influencing law enforcement responses, and affecting how subsequent generations remembered the event through the archival record left behind. Analyzing the framing effect requires comparing coverage of the same event across multiple outlets with different audiences and political affiliations, paying close attention to headline language, photograph selection, and the sequencing of information within an article.
