docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 4: Case Study: Manifest Destiny

docs.title: Two Named Instances of a Pattern You Already Know
docs.text:
Chapter 2 defined systemic oppression as marginalization built into a society's institutions, persisting without requiring an individual villain. This chapter names two specific, extensively documented instances of that pattern inside American government.

Systemic racism is the specific form of systemic oppression in which laws, institutions, and policies produce unequal outcomes for people based on race, regardless of the individual intentions of the officials who administer them. Systemic sexism is the parallel pattern based on gender. Both terms describe outcomes, not just attitudes — a law can be systemically racist in its effects even if the legislators who wrote it never used a racial slur in the process. This chapter's core skill is learning to identify that gap between stated intent and documented effect.

docs.title: Drawing the Lines: Gerrymandering and Redistricting
docs.text:
Every ten years, following the U.S. Census, state governments redraw the boundaries of legislative and congressional districts — a routine, constitutionally required process called redistricting: the periodic redrawing of electoral district boundaries to reflect population changes. Redistricting itself is neutral; how it is done is not automatically neutral.

Gerrymandering is the deliberate manipulation of electoral district boundaries to favor one political party or group, typically by concentrating opposing voters into as few districts as possible ("packing") or spreading them thin across many districts so they cannot form a majority anywhere ("cracking"). Gerrymandering can target political affiliation, but because political affiliation in the U.S. correlates strongly with race in many regions, racial gerrymandering has been used repeatedly to reduce the effective voting power of racial minority communities while remaining technically compliant with one-person-one-vote requirements.

Before we look at how packing and cracking actually redraw a map, it helps to see the two techniques side by side rather than only in the abstract.

docs.title: Diagram: Packing and Cracking District Simulator
docs.text:
Packing and Cracking District Simulator

Type: microsim

sim-id: packing-cracking-district-simulator Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students redraw district boundaries on a simplified grid of voters and see how packing and cracking change election outcomes without changing a single vote.

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) — use the packing/cracking techniques to produce a target outcome. Bloom Verb: demonstrate

Learning objective: Given a fixed grid of voters split 60/40 between two groups, students can draw district boundaries that produce a proportional outcome, then redraw them using packing and cracking to produce a disproportionate outcome — demonstrating that the same voters can produce very different representation depending only on how lines are drawn.

Canvas layout: - Left (450px): a 10x10 grid of colored squares representing voters (blue/orange, fixed 60/40 split, randomized positions) - Right (250px): district boundary tools and a results readout

Interactive controls: - "Draw Boundary" tool: click-drag to group grid squares into districts (5 districts total, must cover all 100 voters) - "Reset Grid" button (keeps the same 60/40 randomized positions) - "Show Proportional Target" toggle: overlays what a proportional outcome (3 blue-majority districts, 2 orange-majority districts) would look like - Results readout: live count of how many districts each color currently wins as boundaries are drawn

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the ungrouped 100-voter grid with its 60/40 split clearly labeled Stage 2: As the student draws each district boundary, show that district's internal vote count and which color currently "wins" it Stage 3: Once all 5 districts are drawn, show the final seat count compared to the proportional target, with the gap (if any) highlighted

Instructional Rationale: An Apply-level objective requires learners to use the technique themselves, not just read about it. Letting students draw their own boundaries and watch the seat count change in real time makes visible what a paragraph of prose can only describe — that gerrymandering requires no vote-count fraud at all, only boundary manipulation.

Default parameters: 60/40 voter split, 5 districts, randomized voter grid on each reset

Implementation: p5.js canvas with a fixed grid of colored cells and a lasso/click-drag district-assignment tool; live vote tally per district recalculated on every boundary change.

docs.title: Barriers Between Citizens and the Ballot
docs.text:
Gerrymandering changes how votes translate into seats. A separate, older set of tactics targets whether a vote gets cast at all. Voter intimidation is the use of threats, harassment, or coercive tactics to discourage eligible voters — historically and disproportionately targeting Black voters and other marginalized groups — from casting a ballot. Voter intimidation is one tool within the broader category of voter suppression: any policy or practice designed to make voting more difficult or impossible for specific groups of eligible voters, whether through intimidation, legal barriers, or administrative obstacles.

Two of the most extensively documented legal tools of 20th-century voter suppression were the poll tax — a fee required to vote, which effectively disenfranchised lower-income citizens, disproportionately Black voters in the post-Reconstruction South — and the literacy test — a requirement that voters demonstrate reading or comprehension skills before registering, administered in a discriminatory and often arbitrary manner to exclude Black voters regardless of their actual literacy. Both tools were race-neutral on paper and applied in a discriminatory manner in practice — a pattern worth remembering the next time a policy is defended as neutral because its text does not mention race.

Sustained organizing against these tools produced the Voting Rights Act of 1965: landmark federal legislation that outlawed literacy tests and other discriminatory voting practices and established federal oversight of jurisdictions with a history of voting discrimination. Before we connect this legislation back to broader civic life, note the pattern across this section: poll tax, literacy test, and gerrymandering all show that voter suppression rarely announces itself by name — it operates through procedures that sound administrative.

Here is a summary comparing the mechanism, era, and legal status of the tools covered so far:

Tool Mechanism Primary Era Legal Status Today Poll tax Financial barrier to voting Post-Reconstruction through 1960s Banned by the 24th Amendment (1964) and Voting Rights Act enforcement Literacy test Comprehension barrier, arbitrarily enforced Post-Reconstruction through 1960s Banned by the Voting Rights Act (1965) Voter intimidation Threats and coercion Ongoing, documented historically and in recent elections Illegal, but enforcement varies Gerrymandering Boundary manipulation Ongoing Partially restricted; racial gerrymandering is illegal, partisan gerrymandering is contested

The stakes of these tools become clear once you connect them to what voting actually protects: civic participation, the broad range of activities — voting, attending public meetings, contacting elected officials, organizing — through which citizens engage with and influence their government. Every barrier this section has described was designed to narrow civic participation for a specific group, not to eliminate voting altogether.

docs.title: How Government Is Talked About
docs.text:
Government representation is shaped not only by who can vote, but by how citizens are persuaded to think about candidates, policies, and institutions. Political persuasion is the deliberate use of rhetoric, argument, and messaging to influence citizens' beliefs or actions regarding government and policy. Political persuasion often draws on ideology in media — the tendency of news and political media to reflect, consciously or not, a particular set of political values and assumptions in how a story is selected, framed, and presented (Chapter 8 examines media bias more broadly; here, the focus is specifically political).

One especially powerful persuasive tool is the emotional appeal: a rhetorical strategy that seeks to influence political belief or action primarily through emotion — fear, anger, pride, or hope — rather than through factual evidence or logical argument. Emotional appeals are not automatically dishonest, but because they bypass careful evaluation of evidence, they are especially effective at reinforcing existing stereotypes and prejudice (Chapter 2) without requiring new facts.

The cumulative effect of voter suppression, gerrymandering, and persuasive media shapes government trust: the degree of confidence citizens hold that government institutions will treat them fairly and represent their interests. Government trust is not uniform across a population — a community with a documented history of voter suppression and gerrymandering has good reason for lower government trust than a community without that history, which is itself an important, often overlooked, data point when interpreting differences in civic participation.

docs.title: Government Representation the Standard Curriculum Often Skips
docs.text:
Most civics instruction treats "government representation" as a story about federal, state, and local levels — and stops there. This course adds a fourth layer that the standard curriculum in Minnesota and nationally has historically underrepresented: tribal sovereignty, the inherent authority of Indigenous tribal nations to govern themselves, make their own laws, and manage their own affairs, independent of state governments and predating the founding of the United States.

Tribal sovereignty is not a grant from the federal government — it is a pre-existing authority that treaties and federal law have recognized, and at times violated, but did not create. This distinction underlies nation-to-nation relations: the formal, government-to-government relationship between the United States (or individual states) and federally recognized tribal nations, conducted through treaties, consultation requirements, and direct negotiation rather than through the ordinary state or local government hierarchy. Minnesota state standard 9.1.6.2, which this course is built to satisfy, specifically asks students to compare these trust relationships between Tribal Nations and Minnesota's state and local governments — Chapter 9 returns to this relationship in much greater depth.

Nation-to-nation relations depend on a concept familiar from geography but politically loaded here: a political boundary, a line establishing the limit of a government's territorial authority, whether between nations, states, or tribal and non-tribal land. Political boundaries around tribal land have shifted repeatedly throughout U.S. history — often through the same land dispossession mechanism Chapter 4 examined — which is why treaty rights (Chapter 9) remain an active legal and political issue today rather than a settled historical matter.

Finally, this chapter closes with a concept that widens the frame beyond any single nation: supranationalism, the transfer of some governing authority from individual nation-states to a larger international body, such as the United Nations or the European Union, that exercises authority across national political boundaries. Supranationalism matters to this course because it shows that political boundaries themselves are not fixed or natural — they are negotiated and renegotiated, the same insight Chapter 3 applied to social categories like race, now applied to territory and governance.

docs.title: Diagram: Four Layers of Government Representation
docs.text:
Four Layers of Government Representation

Type: graph-model

sim-id: four-layers-of-government-representation Library: vis-network Status: Specified

Purpose: Show tribal, local, state, and federal government as four distinct, interacting layers of representation, with tribal sovereignty positioned as independent authority rather than a subset of state government.

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) — explain the relationship between tribal sovereignty and other levels of government. Bloom Verb: explain

Learning objective: Students can explain why tribal nations are described as having a nation-to-nation relationship with the federal government, rather than being classified under state or local government.

Node types: 1. Federal Government (large blue circle, center-top) 2. State Government (medium orange circle) 3. Local Government (small orange circle, connected to State) 4. Tribal Nation (medium green circle, connected directly to Federal, NOT to State) — properties: name (example tribal nation used for illustration), governing authority, treaty status

Edge types: 1. "Constitutional Authority" (solid black arrow, Federal → State) 2. "Delegated Authority" (solid black arrow, State → Local) 3. "Nation-to-Nation Relationship" (double-headed solid green arrow, Federal ↔ Tribal Nation) — distinct styling from the other edges to visually reinforce that this is not a delegation relationship 4. "Consultation Requirement" (dashed green arrow, Tribal Nation → State, labeled with a note that this is a limited, specific-purpose relationship, not general authority)

Layout: Hierarchical, with Tribal Nation positioned at the same vertical level as State Government but visually separated to the side, connected upward directly to Federal

Interactive features: - Hover any node: show its properties in a tooltip - Click any node: highlight all its direct connections and open a side panel with the node's full definition - Click the "Nation-to-Nation Relationship" edge: open an infobox explaining why this relationship is legally and historically distinct from federal-state or state-local delegation

Legend: Node color key (blue = federal, orange = state/local, green = tribal) and edge style key (solid = direct authority, dashed = limited/specific relationship)

Implementation: vis-network with a hierarchical layout option disabled for the Tribal Nation node's horizontal position (custom fixed positioning) so it renders beside, not beneath, State Government.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Systemic racism and systemic sexism describe documented patterns of unequal outcome in government institutions, independent of any individual official's stated intent.
  • Gerrymandering manipulates district boundaries; voter intimidation, voter suppression, the poll tax, and the literacy test manipulate who can vote at all — the Voting Rights Act was built specifically to curtail the latter set of tools.
  • Political persuasion, ideology in media, and the emotional appeal shape how citizens perceive government, with direct consequences for government trust and civic participation.
  • Tribal sovereignty and nation-to-nation relations are a fourth layer of government representation, independent of state authority, built on shifting political boundaries — a pattern of negotiated, not fixed, authority that supranationalism shows operating at the international scale too.

Chapter 6 follows the same systemic pattern into a different domain: how economic policy has excluded specific groups from wealth and opportunity.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Government Representation and Systemic Bias
docs.text: Test your understanding of systemic bias in government representation, voting rights, and tribal sovereignty with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is gerrymandering, as defined in this chapter?
docs.text:
1. The periodic, routine redrawing of district boundaries required after every U.S. Census
  2. A fee required to vote that disenfranchises lower-income citizens
  3. The deliberate manipulation of electoral district boundaries to favor one political party or group, typically through "packing" or "cracking"
  4. A requirement that voters demonstrate reading comprehension before registering
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Gerrymandering is the deliberate manipulation of district boundaries to favor one group, achieved by concentrating opposing voters into few districts (packing) or spreading them thin across many (cracking). Option A describes redistricting, the neutral process gerrymandering exploits. Option B describes the poll tax. Option D describes the literacy test, a separate voter-suppression tool.

Concept Tested: Gerrymandering

docs.title: 2. What did the poll tax and literacy test have in common, according to this chapter?
docs.text:
1. Both explicitly named race in their legal text
  2. Both were race-neutral on paper but applied in a discriminatory manner in practice to exclude Black voters
  3. Both were created by the Voting Rights Act of 1965
  4. Both applied only to voters running for elected office
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter emphasizes that both tools were race-neutral on paper — a fee and a comprehension requirement — yet were administered in a discriminatory manner to exclude Black voters regardless of actual ability to pay or read. Option A is the opposite of how these laws were written. Option C reverses the relationship: the Voting Rights Act banned these tools rather than creating them. Option D misapplies both tools to a context they were not designed for.

Concept Tested: Literacy Test

docs.title: 3. Why does the chapter say a law can be "systemically racist in its effects" even if the officials who wrote it never used a racial slur?
docs.text:
1. Because systemic racism describes documented unequal outcomes produced by laws and institutions, regardless of the individual intentions of the officials who administer them
  2. Because systemic racism requires proof that every official involved held explicitly racist beliefs
  3. Because the term only applies to laws passed before the Voting Rights Act of 1965
  4. Because systemic racism and individual prejudice are defined as exactly the same thing
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Systemic racism describes outcomes, not just attitudes: a law can produce unequal outcomes based on race even when no individual involved expressed explicit racial intent, which is why this chapter's core skill is identifying the gap between stated intent and documented effect. Option B wrongly requires proof of individual belief. Option C invents a time restriction not in the text. Option D collapses a structural concept into a personal one, contradicting Chapter 2's distinction.

Concept Tested: Systemic Racism

docs.title: 4. What did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 accomplish?
docs.text:
1. It established the requirement for a poll tax nationwide
  2. It created the tribal sovereignty doctrine for the first time
  3. It authorized states to redraw district boundaries every ten years
  4. It outlawed literacy tests and other discriminatory voting practices and established federal oversight of jurisdictions with a history of voting discrimination
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Voting Rights Act was landmark federal legislation that outlawed literacy tests and similar discriminatory practices while establishing federal oversight of jurisdictions with a documented history of voting discrimination. Option A reverses the Act's purpose, since it worked against such barriers. Option B misattributes tribal sovereignty, which the chapter describes as pre-existing, not created by this Act. Option C describes redistricting, an unrelated constitutional process.

Concept Tested: Voting Rights Act

docs.title: 5. How does the chapter distinguish tribal sovereignty from nation-to-nation relations?
docs.text:
1. Tribal sovereignty is the inherent, pre-existing authority of tribal nations to govern themselves, while nation-to-nation relations describes the formal government-to-government relationship through which that authority is recognized and negotiated with the United States
  2. Tribal sovereignty was granted by the federal government in 1965, while nation-to-nation relations predates the United States
  3. The two terms describe the exact same legal concept with no meaningful distinction
  4. Tribal sovereignty applies only to state governments, while nation-to-nation relations applies only to the federal government
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Tribal sovereignty is the inherent, pre-existing authority of tribal nations, not a grant from the federal government, while nation-to-nation relations describes the formal treaty-based, government-to-government process through which that authority is recognized and negotiated. Option B reverses which concept predates the United States. Option C denies a distinction the chapter draws explicitly. Option D misassigns both terms to the wrong level of government.

Concept Tested: Tribal Sovereignty

docs.title: 6. A state's voters are split 60/40 between two groups. Mapmakers draw five districts so that the minority group forms a narrow majority in four of the five districts, while the majority group is heavily concentrated into the fifth. Which technique does this scenario apply?
docs.text:
1. Redistricting, because this is simply the routine, neutral process required after a census
  2. A poll tax, because financial barriers determined the outcome
  3. Supranationalism, because authority is being transferred to an international body
  4. Cracking, because the majority group's voters are packed into as few districts as possible while the minority group's votes are spread to control more districts
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. This scenario applies packing and cracking: concentrating one group's voters into a small number of districts (packing) while spreading the other group thinly enough to win a majority in most remaining districts (cracking) — changing seat outcomes without changing a single vote. Option A ignores the deliberate manipulation described, which is not neutral redistricting. Options B and C introduce unrelated tools that do not involve district-boundary manipulation.

Concept Tested: Gerrymandering

docs.title: 7. A 1950s state law requires all voters to pass a reading comprehension test before registering, with no mention of race anywhere in its text. Local officials apply the test inconsistently, failing nearly all Black applicants while passing nearly all white applicants regardless of ability. Which concept does this scenario illustrate?
docs.text:
1. Tribal sovereignty, because the law involves government authority over a territory
  2. Gerrymandering, because the law affects election outcomes
  3. The literacy test functioning as voter suppression — a race-neutral procedure applied in a discriminatory manner to exclude Black voters
  4. Supranationalism, because the law was applied inconsistently across jurisdictions
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. This scenario is a direct application of the chapter's literacy test example: a facially race-neutral requirement, arbitrarily and discriminatorily enforced to exclude Black voters regardless of their actual literacy, making it a documented tool of voter suppression. Option A misapplies a concept about tribal governing authority. Option B misapplies a concept about district-boundary manipulation, not eligibility barriers. Option D misapplies a concept about international governance.

Concept Tested: Voter Suppression

docs.title: 8. A political ad shows dramatic imagery designed to provoke fear about an opposing candidate, offering no statistics or policy comparisons. Which concept from this chapter does the ad most directly apply?
docs.text:
1. Redistricting, because the ad concerns an election
  2. Emotional appeal, because it seeks to influence political belief primarily through fear rather than factual evidence or logical argument
  3. Civic participation, because it encourages viewers to vote
  4. Political boundary, because it defines a jurisdiction's authority
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An emotional appeal is a rhetorical strategy that influences political belief or action primarily through emotion, such as fear, rather than through evidence or logical argument, and the chapter notes such appeals are especially effective at reinforcing existing stereotypes without new facts. Option A misapplies a concept about district boundaries. Option C describes a possible effect, not what the ad's technique is. Option D misapplies a concept about territorial authority.

Concept Tested: Emotional Appeal

docs.title: 9. Why does the chapter argue that lower government trust in a community with a documented history of voter suppression and gerrymandering is "an important, often overlooked, data point"?
docs.text:
1. Because government trust is randomly distributed across communities with no relationship to historical experience
  2. Because lower trust in such a community reflects a rational response to documented barriers, rather than an unrelated or irrational attitude that should be dismissed when interpreting differences in civic participation
  3. Because government trust and civic participation are entirely unrelated concepts
  4. Because the Voting Rights Act eliminated all historical effects of voter suppression immediately upon passage
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter argues that a community with a documented history of voter suppression and gerrymandering has good reason for lower government trust, meaning that trust differences are not random or irrational but connect logically to documented institutional history — a factor that should inform, not be dismissed from, interpretations of civic participation gaps. Option A denies this causal link. Option C contradicts the chapter's explicit connection between trust and participation. Option D overstates the Act's immediate effect on trust.

Concept Tested: Government Trust

docs.title: 10. The chapter connects supranationalism to Chapter 3's insight about social categories. What is the shared insight being applied across both chapters?
docs.text:
1. That political boundaries and social categories are both fixed, natural facts that societies simply discover
  2. That supranationalism and social construction are unrelated concepts with no common thread
  3. That political boundaries, like social categories such as race, are negotiated and renegotiated by human decisions rather than fixed or natural
  4. That international bodies like the United Nations have no real authority over national political boundaries
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter explicitly draws a parallel: just as Chapter 3 showed racial categories were built and rebuilt by human decisions, supranationalism shows that political boundaries are also negotiated and renegotiated rather than fixed or natural, since some governing authority can shift from nation-states to larger international bodies. Option A states the opposite of both chapters' arguments. Option B denies the explicit connection the text draws. Option D contradicts the definition of supranationalism given in the chapter.

Concept Tested: Supranationalism

docs.title: References: Government Representation and Systemic Bias
docs.text:
1. Gerrymandering - Wikipedia - Traces the practice from its 1812 Massachusetts origin through modern "cracking" and "packing" techniques and current reform proposals. Supports the chapter's treatment of gerrymandering and redistricting as tools of systemic bias.

  2. Voting Rights Act of 1965 - Wikipedia - Details the Act's core provisions, its legislative history, and the Supreme Court decisions like Shelby County v. Holder that later weakened it. Anchors the chapter's discussion of the law meant to curtail voter suppression.

  3. Voter suppression in the United States - Wikipedia - Documents poll taxes, literacy tests, and modern suppression tactics with specific historical cases and state-by-state examples. Directly supports the chapter's core vocabulary of exclusionary voting practices.

  4. One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression Is Destroying Our Democracy - Carol Anderson - Bloomsbury Publishing - A National Book Award finalist tracing voter suppression from Reconstruction to the present, giving students a sustained historical argument to pair with the chapter's civics vocabulary.

  5. Give Us the Ballot: The Modern Struggle for Voting Rights in America - Ari Berman - Farrar, Straus and Giroux - A history of the Voting Rights Act's passage and erosion, providing depth on the legislative battles the chapter introduces in survey form.

  6. Fighting Voter Suppression - ACLU - Describes current voter suppression tactics such as voter ID laws, roll purges, and cuts to early voting, and the ACLU's litigation against them, updating the chapter's historical examples with contemporary cases.

  7. Congress and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 - National Archives - Covers the legislative history and immediate impact of the Voting Rights Act, including registration data from 1965-1967, supplementing the chapter's account of the Act's passage.

  8. Tribal Nations & the United States: An Introduction - National Congress of American Indians - Explains tribal sovereignty and the nation-to-nation relationship between tribal governments and the federal government, directly supporting the chapter's treatment of a category of representation civics courses often omit.

  9. Most Americans Don't Feel Strongly About Redistricting - Pew Research Center - Survey data showing most Americans oppose partisan gerrymandering while few understand redistricting processes, giving students current public-opinion evidence for the chapter's discussion of civic participation and trust.

  10. Laws and Court Cases - National Archives - A curated overview of the legal history of Black voting rights from Reconstruction through the Voting Rights Act, connecting the chapter's poll tax and literacy test examples to their eventual legal reversal.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter traces economic exclusion from policy to outcome: embargoes and trade restrictions, redlining and housing discrimination, and bias in college admissions including legacy admissions. Students connect these mechanisms to the wealth gap, community disinvestment, gentrification, and unequal access to credit, and evaluate reparations as one proposed response to racial capitalism's compounding effects.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 15 concepts from the learning graph:

  1. Economic Exclusion
  2. Embargo
  3. Trade Restriction
  4. Redlining
  5. Housing Discrimination
  6. Wealth Gap
  7. College Admissions Bias
  8. Legacy Admissions
  9. Economic Mobility
  10. Racial Capitalism
  11. Labor Exploitation
  12. Reparations
  13. Community Disinvestment
  14. Gentrification
  15. Access To Credit

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 5: Government Representation and Systemic Bias

docs.title: Economic Exclusion as a Category
docs.text:
Chapter 2 defined systemic oppression in general terms. This chapter examines its economic form directly: economic exclusion, the systematic denial of a group's access to wealth-building opportunities — property ownership, credit, employment, education — through policy, institutional practice, or market discrimination. Economic exclusion rarely announces its target by name. Like the poll tax and literacy test from Chapter 5, it usually operates through policies that read as neutral, applied in ways that are not.

This chapter examines economic exclusion at two scales: between nations, and within them.

docs.title: Economic Exclusion Between Nations
docs.text: At the international scale, governments can restrict economic exchange as a matter of foreign policy. An embargo is a government-imposed ban on trade or other economic activity with a specific country or group, typically used as a political or economic sanction. An embargo is one specific type of the broader category trade restriction: any government policy — tariffs, quotas, embargoes, licensing requirements — that limits the free exchange of goods or services across borders. Trade restrictions can be a legitimate policy tool, but they can also function as a form of economic exclusion when applied selectively to isolate or weaken a specific nation, population, or group's access to global markets. Chapter 10 will return to this international scale when it examines U.S. foreign policy's effect on migration.

docs.title: Economic Exclusion Within a Nation: Housing
docs.text:
The domestic story of economic exclusion in the United States begins with housing policy. Redlining was a discriminatory practice, formalized by federal housing agencies beginning in the 1930s, of denying mortgages or insurance to residents of neighborhoods — color-coded red on official maps — based on the racial or ethnic composition of the neighborhood, regardless of an individual applicant's creditworthiness. Redlining is the clearest documented example in this course of systemic racism translated directly into government-created maps.

Redlining is one specific, historically dated instance of a broader pattern: housing discrimination, the unfair treatment of individuals seeking to buy, rent, or finance housing, based on race, ethnicity, gender, or other protected characteristics. Housing discrimination continued in various forms after redlining was formally outlawed by the Fair Housing Act of 1968 — through practices such as steering (guiding buyers toward or away from certain neighborhoods) and discriminatory appraisal.

Before we see the concrete financial effect of these maps, it helps to name the underlying access problem they created: access to credit, the degree to which individuals or communities can obtain loans, mortgages, and other financial instruments needed to build wealth. Redlining did not just deny individual mortgage applications — it denied entire neighborhoods, for generations, the access to credit that homeownership in a growing economy depends on.

docs.title: Diagram: A Redlined Map, Then and Now
docs.text:
A Redlined Map, Then and Now

Type: map

sim-id: redlined-map-then-and-now Library: Leaflet Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students overlay a historical Home Owners' Loan Corporation redlining map with present-day data (e.g., median home value or tree canopy coverage) for the same city, to see redlining's decades-long effect made visible.

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) — examine the relationship between a historical policy map and present-day outcomes. Bloom Verb: examine

Learning objective: Given a historical redlining map and a present-day data layer for the same city, students can identify the correlation between historical grade and current outcome, and explain at least one mechanism (access to credit) connecting the two.

Geographic scope: A single representative U.S. city (implementation note: use a city with well-documented, publicly available HOLC map data, such as Minneapolis or St. Paul, Minnesota, to connect directly to the course's Minnesota standards)

Locations: Neighborhood polygons color-coded by original 1930s HOLC grade (A=green, B=blue, C=yellow, D=red, matching the original historical color scheme)

Data flows: N/A (this is a layered map, not a flow map)

Interactive controls: - Opacity slider to blend the historical grade layer with a present-day data layer - Toggle to switch the present-day layer between two datasets (e.g., median home value, tree canopy percentage) - Click any neighborhood polygon to open an infobox showing its 1930s grade, the original HOLC surveyor's stated rationale (drawn from the historical record), and its current value for the selected present-day dataset

Labels: HOLC grade legend (A/B/C/D), present-day dataset legend

Color scheme: Original HOLC four-color scale for the historical layer; a separate sequential color scale (e.g., light-to-dark blue) for whichever present-day dataset is selected

Interactive features: hover for a quick tooltip (grade + current value), click for the full infobox with historical rationale text

Implementation: Leaflet.js with two GeoJSON layers (historical HOLC polygons, present-day data polygons) and a blend/opacity control.

docs.title: From Housing to the Wealth Gap
docs.text:
Homeownership has historically been the primary way American families build intergenerational wealth. Because redlining and housing discrimination denied that path to specific communities for decades, their effects compound over time into a measurable wealth gap: the persistent difference in accumulated assets — savings, home equity, investments — between demographic groups, which is significantly larger than the income gap between the same groups because wealth compounds across generations while income resets each year. This distinction between income and wealth matters: two families with identical current incomes can have dramatically different wealth if one family's grandparents were able to buy a home in the 1950s and one family's were not.

Redlining also produced community disinvestment: the systematic withdrawal or withholding of public and private investment — infrastructure, business lending, school funding — from a neighborhood, often as a direct consequence of that neighborhood's redlined status. Community disinvestment is why redlining's effects extend beyond individual mortgage denials into decades of underfunded schools, fewer businesses, and deferred infrastructure maintenance in the same neighborhoods.

Decades of disinvestment can eventually make a neighborhood's low property values attractive to outside investment, producing gentrification: the process by which rising property values and new investment in a historically disinvested neighborhood displace long-term, often lower-income residents who can no longer afford to live there. Gentrification presents a genuine analytical puzzle worth sitting with: the same underlying force — capital flowing into a neighborhood — can look like investment from one vantage point and displacement from another, and both descriptions can be accurate for different residents of the same block.

docs.title: Economic Exclusion in Education and Work
docs.text:
Economic exclusion extends beyond housing into the institutions meant to provide upward mobility. College admissions bias describes practices in college and university admissions that systematically disadvantage applicants from marginalized or lower-income backgrounds, even when those practices are not explicitly based on race. The most extensively documented example is legacy admissions: the practice of giving preferential admissions consideration to applicants whose relatives attended the same institution, which disproportionately benefits historically advantaged groups because those groups had greater historical access to elite institutions in the first place.

Notice the mechanism in that last sentence: legacy admissions is race-neutral in its stated criterion (the applicant's own family history), exactly like the poll tax and literacy test from Chapter 5 — and produces a racially disparate outcome because it uses a past era's unequal access as its current baseline.

Economic exclusion in the workplace takes the form of labor exploitation: the practice of extracting excessive value from workers' labor through inadequate wages, unsafe conditions, or denial of workplace protections, disproportionately affecting marginalized workers with less bargaining power. Together, biased admissions and labor exploitation shape a population's economic mobility: the ability of an individual or family to improve their economic position — income, wealth, occupation — relative to the position of their parents or their own starting point. Economic mobility is the outcome all of this chapter's mechanisms ultimately act on; each barrier examined so far narrows it for a specific group.

docs.title: Naming the System and a Proposed Response
docs.text:
This chapter's authors use a specific term for the way these mechanisms interact rather than operate independently: racial capitalism, the analysis that capitalism as an economic system has historically developed by extracting extra value specifically from racialized and marginalized groups — through slavery, colonization, labor exploitation, and exclusion from credit and property — rather than treating racial exclusion as incidental to economic development. Racial capitalism is a framework, not a simple claim of intent; it argues that economic exclusion and profit have been structurally linked throughout American economic history, not merely coincidentally related.

Given that framework, one proposed remedy deserves direct evaluation: reparations, proposed compensation — financial, programmatic, or symbolic — intended to redress the cumulative economic harm caused by historical injustices such as slavery, redlining, and other government-sanctioned exclusion. Reparations proposals vary widely in form and scope, and reasonable people evaluate them differently — this course's goal is not to settle the debate, but to ensure you can evaluate reparations proposals with the specific mechanisms (redlining, wealth gap, community disinvestment) this chapter has documented in hand, rather than in the abstract.

Before you evaluate a reparations proposal yourself, trace the full chain this chapter has built.

docs.title: Diagram: The Compounding Chain of Economic Exclusion
docs.text:
The Compounding Chain of Economic Exclusion

Type: workflow

sim-id: compounding-chain-of-economic-exclusion Library: Mermaid Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students trace the full documented chain from a single 1930s policy (redlining) through to a present-day wealth gap, and evaluate where a reparations proposal could intervene.

Bloom Taxonomy: Evaluate (L5) — judge the effectiveness of proposed interventions at different points in a documented causal chain. Bloom Verb: justify

Learning objective: Given the compounding chain from redlining to wealth gap, students can identify at least two points where policy intervention (including reparations) could act, and justify which point would have the largest measurable effect.

Visual style: Mermaid top-to-bottom flowchart with clickable nodes and one branch showing possible intervention points.

Nodes (each clickable with a click directive opening an infobox): 1. "Redlining (1930s)" — infobox: definition and historical dates 2. "Housing Discrimination" — infobox: definition, notes continuation after 1968 3. "Reduced Access to Credit" — infobox: definition and mechanism 4. "Community Disinvestment" — infobox: definition 5. "Wealth Gap (Present Day)" — infobox: definition, notes wealth vs. income distinction 6. Branch node: "Possible Interventions" connected to nodes 2, 3, and 5 with dashed arrows, each labeled with a real policy category (fair housing enforcement, credit access programs, reparations) — infobox on each dashed arrow explains what that intervention targets and at which point in the chain

Interactivity requirement: every node and every labeled intervention arrow has a click directive opening an infobox; hovering any node shows a preview tooltip.

Color coding: red for the originating policy node, orange for the mechanism nodes, dark red for the present-day outcome node, green for the intervention branch.

Implementation: Mermaid flowchart with click handlers on nodes and edges, rendered in an iframe with a JS shim for the infobox panel.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Economic exclusion operates internationally through embargoes and trade restrictions, and domestically through redlining and broader housing discrimination.
  • Housing exclusion compounds over generations into a wealth gap, driven by reduced access to credit and community disinvestment — which can later produce gentrification as investment returns unevenly.
  • College admissions bias, including legacy admissions, and labor exploitation narrow economic mobility in parallel with housing exclusion.
  • Racial capitalism names the claim that these mechanisms are structurally linked, not coincidental; reparations is one proposed response, evaluable using the specific chain this chapter documented.

Chapter 7 turns to a third domain shaped by the same systemic pattern: how criminality itself is defined and enforced.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Economic Exclusion
docs.text: Test your understanding of economic exclusion, redlining, and the wealth gap with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. How does this chapter define redlining?
docs.text:
1. A government-imposed ban on trade with a specific country
  2. The practice of giving preferential college admission to applicants whose relatives attended the same institution
  3. A discriminatory practice, formalized by federal housing agencies beginning in the 1930s, of denying mortgages or insurance based on a neighborhood's racial or ethnic composition, regardless of an individual applicant's creditworthiness
  4. The unfair treatment of individuals seeking to rent housing based on gender
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Redlining was a discriminatory federal housing practice, formalized in the 1930s, that denied mortgages or insurance to entire neighborhoods based on racial or ethnic composition rather than individual creditworthiness, and the chapter calls it the clearest documented example of systemic racism translated directly into government maps. Option A describes an embargo. Option B describes legacy admissions. Option D describes housing discrimination more broadly, the wider category redlining exemplifies.

Concept Tested: Redlining

docs.title: 2. What is legacy admissions, as defined in this chapter?
docs.text:
1. A policy that bans trade with a specific country as a form of sanction
  2. The practice of giving preferential admissions consideration to applicants whose relatives attended the same institution
  3. A federal law that outlawed discriminatory mortgage lending in 1968
  4. The systematic withdrawal of investment from a historically redlined neighborhood
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Legacy admissions gives preferential consideration to applicants whose relatives attended the same institution, and the chapter explains this disproportionately benefits historically advantaged groups because they had greater historical access to elite institutions in the first place. Option A describes an embargo. Option C describes the Fair Housing Act, a different policy. Option D describes community disinvestment, an unrelated mechanism.

Concept Tested: Legacy Admissions

docs.title: 3. Why does the chapter say the wealth gap is significantly larger than the income gap between the same demographic groups?
docs.text:
1. Because wealth and income are defined as the exact same measurement
  2. Because income is always higher than wealth for every family regardless of history
  3. Because the wealth gap only measures differences in annual salary
  4. Because wealth compounds across generations while income resets each year, so two families with identical current incomes can have dramatically different wealth depending on past access to homeownership
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter distinguishes wealth, which compounds across generations through assets like home equity, from income, which resets each year — meaning two families with identical current incomes can hold very different wealth depending on whether earlier generations could buy a home. Option A collapses a distinction the chapter draws carefully. Option B makes an unsupported blanket claim. Option C misdefines wealth gap as an income measurement.

Concept Tested: Wealth Gap

docs.title: 4. What does the chapter mean by describing racial capitalism as "a framework, not a simple claim of intent"?
docs.text:
1. It means racial capitalism argues that economic exclusion and profit have been structurally linked throughout American economic history, rather than claiming individual capitalists intended racial harm
  2. It means racial capitalism has been legally proven in every U.S. court
  3. It means racial capitalism only applies to trade restrictions between nations
  4. It means racial capitalism denies that slavery or redlining had any economic effect
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Racial capitalism analyzes how capitalism as a system has structurally extracted extra value from racialized and marginalized groups through mechanisms like slavery and redlining, treating this as a structural pattern rather than a claim about any individual's intent. Option B overstates the framework as a legal finding. Option C wrongly narrows its scope to international trade. Option D contradicts the framework's central claim about the economic effects of exclusion.

Concept Tested: Racial Capitalism

docs.title: 5. What "genuine analytical puzzle" does the chapter identify in gentrification?
docs.text:
1. Gentrification never actually involves any change in property values
  2. Gentrification only occurs in neighborhoods that were never subject to redlining
  3. The same underlying force — capital flowing into a historically disinvested neighborhood — can accurately look like investment from one vantage point and displacement from another, for different residents of the same block
  4. Gentrification and community disinvestment describe identical, interchangeable processes
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter frames gentrification as a genuine puzzle because the same capital inflow into a historically disinvested neighborhood can be accurately described as investment by some observers and as displacement by long-term, lower-income residents who can no longer afford to stay — both descriptions can be true at once. Option A denies gentrification's defining feature. Option B contradicts the chapter's account of gentrification following disinvestment. Option D collapses two distinct, sequential concepts into one.

Concept Tested: Gentrification

docs.title: 6. A government bans all trade and economic activity with a specific country as a political sanction. Which concept does this scenario apply?
docs.text:
1. Redlining, because it involves denying access to a resource
  2. Gentrification, because it involves economic change in a defined area
  3. Legacy admissions, because it involves preferential treatment
  4. An embargo, a government-imposed ban on trade or economic activity with a specific country, typically used as a political or economic sanction
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. This scenario is a direct application of the chapter's definition of an embargo: a government-imposed ban on trade or economic activity with a specific country, used as a political or economic sanction, and one specific type of the broader category of trade restriction. Option A misapplies a concept about domestic housing policy. Option B misapplies a concept about neighborhood-level investment. Option C misapplies a concept about educational admissions.

Concept Tested: Embargo

docs.title: 7. A university admits an applicant partly because the applicant's parent and grandparent both attended the school, without ever mentioning the applicant's race in its criteria. Applying the chapter's analysis, why can this still produce a racially disparate outcome?
docs.text:
1. Because the policy is race-neutral in its stated criterion but uses a past era's unequal access to elite institutions as its current baseline, similar to the poll tax and literacy test
  2. Because the university's admissions office has stated an explicitly racist intent
  3. Because legacy admissions is illegal in every U.S. state
  4. Because the applicant's own personal achievements are entirely irrelevant to the decision
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter draws a direct parallel between legacy admissions and Chapter 5's poll tax and literacy test: all three are race-neutral in their stated criteria yet produce racially disparate outcomes because they use a baseline shaped by a past era's unequal access. Option B invents an explicit intent the scenario does not describe. Option C is factually incorrect. Option D overstates the scenario, which describes one factor among several.

Concept Tested: Legacy Admissions

docs.title: 8. Using the documented chain this chapter builds — from redlining to reduced credit access to community disinvestment to the present-day wealth gap — which statement reflects a defensible way to evaluate a reparations proposal?
docs.text:
1. Reparations proposals cannot be evaluated because the chapter provides no documented mechanisms connecting historical policy to present outcomes
  2. Reparations proposals should be evaluated against the specific documented mechanisms, such as redlining and community disinvestment, that produced the wealth gap, rather than debated only in the abstract
  3. Reparations proposals are only about individual behavior and have no connection to historical policy
  4. Reparations proposals should be evaluated solely by comparing this year's income between groups
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's stated goal is to equip readers to evaluate reparations proposals using the specific documented chain — redlining, reduced credit access, community disinvestment, wealth gap — rather than debating the concept only in the abstract. Option A contradicts the extensive documented chain the chapter provides. Option C ignores the chapter's structural framing. Option D wrongly substitutes income, which the chapter distinguishes from wealth, as the sole measure.

Concept Tested: Reparations

docs.title: 9. Why does the chapter compare legacy admissions directly to the poll tax and literacy test from Chapter 5?
docs.text:
1. Because all three tools were declared unconstitutional in the same court case
  2. Because all three tools apply only to voting rather than to education or housing
  3. Because all three tools are stated in race-neutral terms yet produce racially disparate outcomes by using a baseline built from a prior era's unequal access
  4. Because all three tools are entirely unrelated and the comparison is only coincidental
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter draws this comparison specifically because all three mechanisms are race-neutral in their stated criteria — family history, ability to pay, or a comprehension test — yet each produces racially disparate outcomes by relying on a baseline shaped by prior, unequal access. Option A invents a shared legal history the chapter does not claim. Option B is factually wrong, since legacy admissions concerns education, not voting. Option D denies the explicit structural parallel the chapter draws.

Concept Tested: College Admissions Bias

docs.title: 10. Analyzing the chain this chapter describes, why does community disinvestment following redlining eventually make a neighborhood a candidate for gentrification?
docs.text:
1. Because community disinvestment has no measurable effect on property values over time
  2. Because decades of withheld investment can depress a neighborhood's property values to the point that they become attractive to new, outside capital, which then drives the property-value increases associated with gentrification
  3. Because gentrification and redlining occur simultaneously in the same year
  4. Because community disinvestment only affects school funding and has no connection to housing markets
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter traces a causal chain: redlining produces community disinvestment, which depresses property values over decades, which can eventually make that same low-cost neighborhood attractive to outside investment — the rising property values and new investment that define gentrification. Option A denies the very mechanism the chapter documents. Option C ignores the multi-decade gap the chapter describes between these events. Option D wrongly narrows disinvestment's scope, contradicting the chapter's list of infrastructure, business lending, and schools.

Concept Tested: Community Disinvestment

docs.title: References: Economic Exclusion
docs.text:
1. Redlining - Wikipedia - Traces redlining from 1930s federal housing policy through its contemporary digital and environmental forms, with wealth-gap statistics tied directly to HOLC maps. Anchors the chapter's central mechanism of economic exclusion.

  2. Racial wealth gap in the United States - Wikipedia - Explains how housing, employment, education, and credit access compound over generations to produce today's wealth gap, with historical data from 1984 onward. Supports the chapter's argument about compounding economic consequences.

  3. Reparations for slavery - Wikipedia - Surveys reparations proposals, debates, and international precedents, including quantified estimates and opposing arguments. Gives students the full range of positions the chapter asks them to evaluate.

  4. The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America - Richard Rothstein - Liveright Publishing - A definitive account of how federal, state, and local policy deliberately created residential segregation, providing the policy history behind this chapter's redlining and housing discrimination discussion.

  5. Evicted: Poverty and Profit in the American City - Matthew Desmond - Crown Publishing - A Pulitzer Prize-winning ethnography of housing instability and eviction in low-income communities, grounding the chapter's housing discrimination and community disinvestment concepts in lived experience.

  6. Mapping Inequality - University of Richmond Digital Scholarship Lab - An interactive archive of the original 1930s HOLC redlining maps for cities nationwide, letting students examine the primary source documents behind the chapter's redlining discussion.

  7. Wealth Gaps Within Racial and Ethnic Groups - Pew Research Center - Current data on wealth disparities between Black, Hispanic, Asian, and White households, including how the gap varies by income level, updating the chapter's wealth-gap discussion with recent figures.

  8. Who Uses Legacy Admissions? - Brookings Institution - Analyzes how widespread legacy admissions are across selective and public colleges and their overlap with race-conscious admissions, directly supporting the chapter's college admissions bias discussion.

  9. Black Wealth Is Increasing, But So Is the Racial Wealth Gap - Brookings Institution - Examines economic mobility trends alongside a persistently widening wealth gap, giving students evidence for the chapter's distinction between individual mobility and systemic exclusion.

  10. HOLC "Redlining" Maps: The Persistent Structure of Segregation and Economic Inequality - National Community Reinvestment Coalition - Connects historical redlining maps to present-day patterns of community disinvestment and gentrification, supporting the chapter's link between historical policy and current neighborhood change.

docs.title: The Justice System and the Construction of Criminality
Summary
docs.text: Students examine criminality as a social construction rather than a fixed category, tracing how codes and laws are selectively enforced and how that enforcement produces sentencing disparities, mass incarceration, and the school-to-prison pipeline. The chapter covers racial profiling, implicit bias, and prejudice statistics as evidence, and introduces restorative justice and due process as alternative and corrective frameworks to the patterns students identify.

  8. Racial Profiling
  9. School-To-Prison Pipeline
