docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 6: Economic Exclusion

docs.title: Is "Criminal" a Fact or a Label?
docs.text:
Ask most people what makes an act a crime, and they will describe something close to common sense: crimes are acts that harm people, and the law simply names them. This chapter asks you to examine that assumption more carefully, using the same social-construction lens Chapter 3 applied to race.

Criminality is the status of being classified, by a legal system, as having committed an act the system defines as a crime. Notice the wording: criminality is a classification, not an inherent property of a person or even, necessarily, of an act. The same behavior — possessing a small amount of a substance, for instance — has been legal in one U.S. state and a felony in a neighboring state in the same year. That variation is only possible if criminality is, at least in part, socially constructed in the sense Chapter 3 defined: built by a society's decisions, not discovered as a fixed natural fact.

This course names that specific application of social construction the social construction of crime: the recognition that what counts as a crime — and how seriously it is punished — reflects social and political decisions about which harms matter and which groups' behavior is treated as threatening, rather than a fixed, universal moral category. The social construction of crime does not claim that no act is genuinely harmful. It claims that the line between "criminal" and "not criminal," and the severity attached to each side of that line, is drawn by people, with all the historical biases this course has already documented.

docs.title: From Codes and Laws to Selective Enforcement
docs.text:
The social construction of crime becomes concrete through codes and laws: the formal, written rules — statutes, ordinances, regulations — through which a government defines prohibited conduct and specifies its penalties. Codes and laws are, in principle, applied equally to everyone they cover. In practice, that principle is frequently violated through selective enforcement: the practice of applying laws more strictly, or more frequently, to some groups than to others, even when the law's text applies equally to all.

Selective enforcement has a documented history worth tracing directly, because policing itself has changed dramatically over time. Policing history refers to the documented evolution of law enforcement institutions in the United States — from early slave patrols in the antebellum South, through the professionalization of municipal police in the early 20th century, to current community and militarized policing models — a history that shapes which communities police forces originated to control and which they originated to protect. Understanding policing history is not an accusation against any individual officer; it is a historical-context step, exactly as Chapter 1 defined that term, necessary before interpreting present-day enforcement patterns.

docs.title: Diagram: Policing History Timeline
docs.text:
Policing History Timeline

Type: timeline

sim-id: policing-history-timeline Library: vis-timeline Status: Specified

Purpose: Show the documented institutional evolution of American policing, providing historical context for later sections on selective enforcement and racial profiling.

Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) — summarize the major institutional shifts in the history of American policing. Bloom Verb: summarize

Learning objective: Students can summarize at least three major institutional shifts in the history of American policing and explain why this history is treated as historical context (Chapter 1) for evaluating present-day enforcement patterns.

Time period: 1700s-present

Events (each clickable with an infobox citing the type of historical source involved): - 1700s-1865: Slave patrols in Southern colonies and states — infobox notes these as among the earliest organized policing institutions in the region, citing state slave-code statutes as a primary source type - 1838-1900s: Formation of professional municipal police departments (Boston 1838 cited as an early example) — infobox notes the primarily order-maintenance and property-protection origins of these forces - 1960s-1970s: Civil rights era confrontations between police and protesters, widely documented on film and in news photography - 1970s-1990s: "War on drugs" era policy shifts and their connection to sentencing policy (previewed here, detailed later in this chapter) - 1990s-2000s: Rise of "broken windows" and zero-tolerance policing strategies - 2010s-present: Body camera adoption and community policing reform efforts following widely documented incidents

Visual style: Horizontal timeline, single row, grouped into shaded eras

Color coding: distinct background shading per era (colonial/slave-patrol era, professionalization era, civil rights era, war-on-drugs era, reform era)

Interactive features: click any event for a detail panel; hover for one-line preview.

Implementation: vis-timeline library with era-grouping background bands and a JSON event dataset.

Selective enforcement does not always come from a conscious decision. Implicit bias — introduced briefly in Chapter 2 as a form of bias — plays a documented role here specifically: unconscious attitudes or stereotypes that affect a person's understanding, actions, and decisions without their awareness, including decisions made by police officers, prosecutors, and judges. Implicit bias helps explain how selective enforcement can occur even among officials who consciously believe they are applying the law equally.

One specific, well-studied form of selective enforcement is racial profiling: the practice of targeting individuals for police suspicion, stops, or searches based on their race or ethnicity rather than on individualized evidence of wrongdoing. Racial profiling has been measured directly through prejudice statistics: data — such as stop rates, search rates, and outcome rates broken down by race — used to measure whether selective enforcement or racial profiling is occurring within a given jurisdiction. Prejudice statistics matter because they convert a claim that could otherwise be dismissed as anecdotal into a testable, measurable pattern — exactly the kind of source corroboration Chapter 1 asked you to seek before trusting a claim.

docs.title: From Enforcement to Outcome
docs.text:
Selective enforcement, once it results in an arrest and conviction, does not stop shaping outcomes. Sentencing disparity is a measurable difference in the length or severity of criminal sentences handed down for comparable offenses, correlated with the defendant's race, class, or other demographic characteristics, even after controlling for the severity of the offense. Sentencing disparity, repeated across millions of cases over decades, is one of the primary documented drivers of mass incarceration: the historically and internationally unusual scale of imprisonment in the United States, both in absolute numbers and as a rate per capita, disproportionately affecting Black and Latino communities.

Before we look at the two protections meant to guard against these outcomes, consider one more concept from the justice system's own vocabulary: due process, the constitutional guarantee that the government must follow fair, established legal procedures before depriving a person of life, liberty, or property. Due process is the formal safeguard the justice system claims to provide against exactly the kind of unequal treatment sentencing disparity and racial profiling document — which is part of why measuring the gap between due process as a formal guarantee and enforcement as a documented practice is a central skill of this chapter.

Here is a summary connecting the chapter's core mechanism terms to what each one measures:

Term What It Measures Where in the Process It Occurs Selective enforcement Whether a law is applied unequally across groups Policing / initial contact Racial profiling Whether suspicion targets race rather than evidence Stop and search decisions Implicit bias Unconscious influence on judgment Any decision point (officer, prosecutor, judge) Sentencing disparity Unequal sentence length for comparable offenses Sentencing Mass incarceration Cumulative scale of imprisonment System-wide outcome

docs.title: Consequences That Extend Beyond the Justice System
docs.text:
Contact with the justice system produces effects that reach beyond any individual sentence. Criminal label impact describes the lasting social and economic consequences a person experiences after being labeled a criminal — reduced employment prospects, housing denial, loss of voting rights in some states — which can persist long after a sentence is completed and regardless of whether the original enforcement was selective or fair. The criminal label, once applied, functions similarly to the erasure and stereotype dynamics Chapter 2 described: it can overwrite every other fact about a person with a single, sticky category.

For young people, these dynamics have a documented specific pathway: the school-to-prison pipeline, the pattern by which harsh school discipline policies — suspension, expulsion, on-campus policing — funnel students, disproportionately Black and Latino students and students with disabilities, out of the education system and into the juvenile or criminal justice system. The school-to-prison pipeline connects directly to juvenile justice: the distinct legal system and set of procedures for handling individuals under 18 accused of crimes, historically premised on rehabilitation but subject to the same documented patterns of racial disparity found in the adult system.

One historical term captures what happens when a person facing unjust or selectively enforced law seeks to escape its reach rather than submit to it: fugitivity, the historical and ongoing practice of evading a legal or social system perceived as illegitimate or unjustly applied, ranging from formerly enslaved people escaping captivity to contemporary forms of resistance to selective enforcement. Fugitivity is not simply "breaking the law" in the ordinary sense — this course's use of the term specifically names evasion of systems whose legitimacy the person evading has reason to question, connecting directly back to the social construction of crime this chapter opened with.

docs.title: Alternatives and Corrections
docs.text: This chapter does not end with only a description of the problem. Restorative justice is an alternative approach to addressing crime that focuses on repairing harm, accountability, and reconciliation between the offender, the victim, and the community, rather than solely on punishment. Restorative justice is one of several concrete proposals, alongside stronger enforcement of due process protections, aimed at addressing the specific patterns of sentencing disparity, mass incarceration, and the school-to-prison pipeline this chapter has documented.

docs.title: Diagram: Sentencing Outcome Comparator
docs.text:
Sentencing Outcome Comparator

Type: microsim

sim-id: sentencing-outcome-comparator Library: Chart.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students compare sentencing-length distributions for a matched, comparable offense across demographic groups, drawn from representative published sentencing-commission data ranges.

Bloom Taxonomy: Evaluate (L5) — assess whether an observed disparity is consistent with a documented pattern of sentencing disparity. Bloom Verb: assess

Learning objective: Given representative sentencing-length data for a single offense category across demographic groups, students can identify whether a disparity exists, describe its size, and assess whether the disparity is consistent with the concept of sentencing disparity as defined in this chapter.

Chart type: Box-and-whisker or grouped bar chart

Purpose: Show the distribution (not just the average) of sentence lengths for a single, held-constant offense category, split by demographic group

X-axis: Demographic group categories (using representative, clearly labeled illustrative ranges consistent with published sentencing-commission reports, not individualized case data) Y-axis: Sentence length in months

Data series: Representative distribution ranges per group for one illustrative offense category, sourced from the general pattern documented in U.S. Sentencing Commission demographic reports

Interactive controls: - Dropdown: select a different (but similarly matched) offense category to compare whether the disparity pattern holds across offense types - Hover any bar or box: reveal the exact numeric range and the source category it represents

Title: "Sentence Length Distribution for a Matched Offense, by Demographic Group"

Annotations: A note clarifying that the offense category and severity are held constant across groups in this illustrative dataset, which is the condition under which "sentencing disparity" as defined in this chapter applies

Implementation: Chart.js box-plot or grouped-bar plugin, reading from a small illustrative dataset file clearly labeled as representative rather than a specific real case.

Before you close this chapter, apply its central distinction to a scenario of your own.

Two people are convicted of the same nonviolent drug offense in the same state. One receives probation; the other receives three years in prison. What would you need to know before concluding this is a sentencing disparity? Click to expand

You would need to confirm the offenses were genuinely comparable — same substance, same quantity, same prior record — since sentencing disparity specifically means unequal outcomes for comparable offenses, not any two different sentences. You would want prejudice statistics showing whether this pattern (harsher sentences for one demographic group, for matched offenses) holds across many cases, not just these two, since a single pair of cases could reflect factors other than disparity. You would also want to know whether due process protections were followed equally in both cases, and whether implicit bias or racial profiling played a documented role earlier in either case's path through the system — from the initial stop through prosecution.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Criminality reflects the social construction of crime — codified into codes and laws, but subject to selective enforcement, a pattern with roots traceable through policing history.
  • Implicit bias and racial profiling help explain how selective enforcement occurs; prejudice statistics provide the evidence to measure it.
  • Sentencing disparity compounds into mass incarceration, despite the formal guarantee of due process.
  • The criminal label carries consequences beyond a sentence, funneled disproportionately through the school-to-prison pipeline into the juvenile justice system; fugitivity names the historical response of evading an unjustly applied system.
  • Restorative justice offers one documented alternative framework aimed at repairing harm rather than only punishing it.

Chapter 8 turns from the justice system to media, examining how the same patterns of bias and stereotype shape who gets represented, and how.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: The Justice System and the Construction of Criminality
docs.text: Test your understanding of criminality, selective enforcement, and the justice system with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. How does this chapter define criminality?
docs.text:
1. A fixed, universal moral property inherent to certain acts regardless of jurisdiction
  2. A synonym for due process
  3. The status of being classified, by a legal system, as having committed an act the system defines as a crime
  4. A measurable statistic tracking arrest rates across states
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Criminality is a classification assigned by a legal system, not an inherent property of a person or act, illustrated by the chapter's example of a substance that is legal in one state and a felony in a neighboring state in the same year. Option A directly contradicts this variability. Option B confuses criminality with an unrelated constitutional guarantee. Option D describes a type of data used to measure enforcement patterns, not the definition of criminality itself.

Concept Tested: Criminality

docs.title: 2. What are codes and laws, as defined in this chapter?
docs.text:
1. The formal, written rules — statutes, ordinances, regulations — through which a government defines prohibited conduct and specifies its penalties
  2. Unconscious attitudes that affect a judge's decisions without their awareness
  3. Data used to measure whether selective enforcement is occurring
  4. The historical evolution of law enforcement institutions in the United States
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Codes and laws are the formal, written rules through which a government defines prohibited conduct and its penalties, and the chapter notes they are, in principle, applied equally even though selective enforcement frequently violates that principle in practice. Option B describes implicit bias. Option C describes prejudice statistics. Option D describes policing history, a separate concept.

Concept Tested: Codes And Laws

docs.title: 3. What does the social construction of crime claim, according to this chapter?
docs.text:
1. That no act is ever genuinely harmful to another person
  2. That every U.S. state defines the same acts as crimes with identical penalties
  3. That criminal law is entirely separate from any social or political decision-making process
  4. That what counts as a crime, and how seriously it is punished, reflects social and political decisions about which harms matter and which groups' behavior is treated as threatening, rather than a fixed, universal moral category
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The social construction of crime holds that the line between criminal and not criminal, and the severity attached to each side, is drawn by people through social and political decisions rather than existing as a fixed, universal category. Option A misstates the claim, since the chapter explicitly says it does not deny real harm exists. Option B is contradicted by the chapter's own example of legal variation across states. Option C denies the very connection the concept asserts.

Concept Tested: Social Construction Of Crime

docs.title: 4. How does the chapter distinguish implicit bias from racial profiling?
docs.text:
1. The two terms describe exactly the same practice with no meaningful difference
  2. Implicit bias is an unconscious attitude that can influence any decision point in the system, while racial profiling is a specific practice of targeting individuals for police suspicion based on race rather than individualized evidence
  3. Racial profiling is legal in all fifty states, while implicit bias is illegal everywhere
  4. Implicit bias only affects judges, while racial profiling only affects police officers
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Implicit bias is an unconscious attitude that can affect any decision point — officer, prosecutor, or judge — without the person's awareness, while racial profiling is the specific, well-studied practice of targeting individuals for stops or searches based on race rather than individualized evidence. Option A denies a distinction the chapter draws explicitly. Option C invents legal statuses not discussed in the text. Option D wrongly restricts both concepts to a single role each.

Concept Tested: Racial Profiling

docs.title: 5. What relationship does the chapter describe between due process and sentencing disparity?
docs.text:
1. Sentencing disparity is legally required under due process protections
  2. Due process and sentencing disparity are unrelated concepts from entirely different fields
  3. Due process is the formal safeguard the justice system claims to provide against unequal treatment, while sentencing disparity is documented evidence of a gap between that formal guarantee and actual practice
  4. Due process only applies to juvenile justice, not to adult sentencing
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Due process is the constitutional guarantee of fair legal procedure, which the justice system claims protects against unequal treatment, while sentencing disparity is measurable evidence of unequal sentence outcomes for comparable offenses — making the gap between the two a central skill this chapter asks students to measure. Option A misstates the relationship as a requirement rather than a claimed protection. Option B denies the explicit connection the chapter draws. Option D invents a restriction not found in the text.

Concept Tested: Due Process

docs.title: 6. Two people are convicted of the same nonviolent drug offense in the same state; one receives probation and the other receives three years in prison. Applying the chapter's guidance, what must be confirmed before concluding this reflects a sentencing disparity?
docs.text:
1. That the offenses were genuinely comparable in substance, quantity, and prior record, and that this pattern holds across many similar cases rather than appearing in just this one pair
  2. Nothing further — any difference in sentence length between two people automatically counts as a sentencing disparity
  3. That both defendants attended the same school as children
  4. That the case occurred after the school-to-prison pipeline was first documented
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter's own worked example stresses confirming the offenses were truly comparable and checking prejudice statistics across many cases, since sentencing disparity specifically means unequal outcomes for comparable offenses documented as a pattern, not simply any two different sentences. Option B skips the comparability check the chapter insists on. Option C introduces an irrelevant factor. Option D confuses an unrelated timeline detail with the actual evidentiary requirement.

Concept Tested: Sentencing Disparity

docs.title: 7. A middle school suspends and eventually involves on-campus police in disciplining a student for a minor infraction, a pattern the school applies disproportionately to Black and Latino students. Which concept does this scenario most directly illustrate?
docs.text:
1. Restorative justice, because the school is repairing harm to the community
  2. Fugitivity, because the student is evading an illegitimate system
  3. Due process, because the student received a fair procedural hearing
  4. The school-to-prison pipeline, the pattern by which harsh school discipline policies funnel students, disproportionately Black and Latino students and students with disabilities, out of the education system and into the juvenile or criminal justice system
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. This scenario is a direct application of the school-to-prison pipeline: harsh discipline policies, including on-campus policing, funneling disproportionately Black and Latino students out of school and into the justice system. Option A misapplies restorative justice, an alternative approach not described here. Option B misapplies fugitivity, which involves the student's own evasion, not the school's disciplinary pattern. Option C misapplies due process, which concerns procedural fairness rather than the funneling pattern itself.

Concept Tested: School-To-Prison Pipeline

docs.title: 8. A person formerly enslaved escapes captivity rather than submit to a legal system built to enforce that captivity. Which concept from this chapter does this action illustrate?
docs.text:
1. Sentencing disparity, because it involves an unequal legal outcome
  2. Fugitivity, the historical and ongoing practice of evading a legal or social system perceived as illegitimate or unjustly applied
  3. Juvenile justice, because it involves a distinct legal system
  4. Prejudice statistics, because it involves measurable data
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Fugitivity names the historical and ongoing practice of evading a legal or social system perceived as illegitimate, ranging from formerly enslaved people escaping captivity to contemporary resistance to selective enforcement — distinct from ordinary lawbreaking because it specifically names evasion of a system whose legitimacy is in question. Option A misapplies a concept about sentence length. Option C misapplies a concept about the youth legal system. Option D misapplies a concept about measurement data.

Concept Tested: Fugitivity

docs.title: 9. Why does the chapter present policing history as necessary background before interpreting present-day enforcement patterns?
docs.text:
1. Because studying policing history is meant as an accusation against individual officers working today
  2. Because policing history has no documented connection to current enforcement patterns
  3. Because understanding the documented evolution of policing institutions — from slave patrols through professionalization to current models — functions as historical context, in the sense Chapter 1 defined that term, for interpreting present-day patterns
  4. Because policing history only covers events that occurred after the year 2000
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter explicitly frames policing history as a historical-context step, as Chapter 1 defined that term, necessary for interpreting present-day enforcement patterns — not an accusation against any individual officer, but background on which communities police forces originated to control versus protect. Option A directly contradicts the chapter's own disclaimer. Option B denies the connection the chapter draws. Option D misstates the timeline, which begins in the 1700s.

Concept Tested: Policing History

docs.title: 10. How does the chapter say criminal label impact functions similarly to the erasure and stereotype dynamics described in Chapter 2?
docs.text:
1. The criminal label, once applied, can overwrite every other fact about a person with a single, sticky category, producing lasting consequences such as reduced employment or housing denial regardless of whether the original enforcement was fair
  2. Criminal label impact has no relationship to any concept introduced in earlier chapters
  3. The criminal label automatically disappears once a person's sentence is completed
  4. Criminal label impact applies only to people who were selectively enforced against, never to anyone else
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter draws a direct parallel to Chapter 2's erasure and stereotype dynamics: a criminal label can overwrite every other fact about a person with one sticky category, producing lasting consequences like reduced employment prospects or housing denial that persist after a sentence ends, regardless of whether the original enforcement was fair. Option B denies the explicit parallel drawn. Option C contradicts the chapter's point that consequences persist "long after a sentence is completed." Option D adds a restriction the definition does not include.

Concept Tested: Criminal Label Impact

docs.text:
1. Mass incarceration in the United States - Wikipedia - Traces the growth of the U.S. prison population from the 1970s "war on drugs" through mandatory minimums, with racial disparity statistics showing Black Americans imprisoned at five times the white rate. Anchors the chapter's central case study.

  2. Racial profiling - Wikipedia - Defines racial profiling and traces its roots to slave patrols, with international comparisons and documented cases. Directly supports the chapter's coverage of selective enforcement and policing history.

  3. School-to-prison pipeline - Wikipedia - Documents how zero-tolerance discipline policies funnel students, disproportionately Black students, out of school and into the justice system, with restorative justice offered as an alternative. Matches the chapter's juvenile justice discussion closely.

  4. The New Jim Crow: Mass Incarceration in the Age of Colorblindness - Michelle Alexander - The New Press - A landmark argument that mass incarceration functions as a racial caste system, providing the chapter's core theoretical framework for criminality as a social construction.

  5. Just Mercy: A Story of Justice and Redemption - Bryan Stevenson - Spiegel & Grau - A memoir by the founder of the Equal Justice Initiative documenting wrongful convictions and sentencing disparities, giving students a case-based complement to the chapter's statistical evidence.

  6. Racial Justice - Equal Justice Initiative - Connects the history of enslavement, lynching, and segregation directly to mass incarceration today, supporting the chapter's argument that current enforcement patterns have deep historical roots.

  7. Criminal Justice Fact Sheet - NAACP - Compiles current incarceration, arrest, and sentencing disparity statistics by race, including juvenile justice data, giving students concrete numbers for the chapter's sentencing disparity discussion.

  8. Mass Incarceration - ACLU - Describes the Campaign for Smart Justice's state-by-state effort to reduce incarceration and address racial disparities in sentencing and policing, supporting the chapter's discussion of policy responses.

  9. Restorative Justice: An Overview - Office of Justice Programs, U.S. Department of Justice - A federal overview of restorative justice principles as an alternative to punitive enforcement, directly supporting the chapter's restorative justice and due process discussion.

  10. Restorative Practices and School Discipline - California Department of Education - Explains how restorative practices reduce reliance on suspension and expulsion in schools, giving students a concrete policy alternative to the school-to-prison pipeline documented earlier in the chapter.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter turns the course's analytical tools on media itself: colorism and beauty standard bias in casting and advertising, headline bias and framing effects in news, and stereotype, tokenized casting, and whitewashing across film and television. Students build media literacy skills — including an introduction to algorithmic and digital media bias — and practice counter-storytelling as a response to propaganda and one-sided framing.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 7: The Justice System and the Construction of Criminality

docs.title: Media as a Site of Representation
docs.text: Every previous chapter in this course has examined institutions — government, the economy, the justice system — through the lens of representation and marginalization. This chapter applies the same lens to an institution students encounter daily, often without thinking of it as an institution at all: media. Media representation is the way films, television, news, advertising, and digital platforms portray different groups, in terms of how frequently they appear, in what roles, and with what accuracy relative to their actual presence and diversity in society. Chapter 2 defined representation in the abstract; this chapter examines its most visible, most studied domain.

docs.title: Colorism and Beauty Standards on Screen
docs.text:
Chapter 3 defined colorism as prejudice or preferential treatment based on skin tone, and the beauty standard as a culturally dominant, historically weighted measure of attractiveness. Media is where both concepts become most visible and most measurable. Colorism in media describes the documented pattern by which lighter-skinned actors, models, and public figures receive more screen time, more favorable lighting, and more leading roles than darker-skinned counterparts within the same demographic group. Beauty standard bias describes the media industry's persistent favoring of a narrow beauty standard — often reflecting historically dominant racial and body-type norms — in casting, advertising, and editorial choices, even as audiences themselves grow more diverse.

Before comparing these two closely related patterns side by side, it's worth being precise about how they differ: colorism in media operates specifically along the lightness/darkness axis within groups, while beauty standard bias is the broader phenomenon of a single narrow standard — encompassing body type, facial features, and hair texture along with skin tone — being treated as universally attractive.

docs.title: Bias in the News: Headlines and Framing
docs.text:
Fictional and commercial media are not the only site of bias — news media, which claims a standard of objectivity that entertainment media does not, has its own documented patterns. Headline bias is the tendency of news headlines to use different language — active versus passive voice, sympathetic versus criminalizing word choice — depending on the race, nationality, or social group of the people involved in the story, even when the underlying facts are identical. A now well-documented example: identical property crimes described with words like "looting" for one group and "finding supplies" for another, based only on who is pictured.

Headline bias is one visible symptom of a broader phenomenon: the framing effect, the way a story's selection of details, word choices, and visual context shapes audience interpretation of an event, independent of whether any individual fact reported is false. Framing does not require lying. Two entirely accurate news stories about the same event can produce opposite audience impressions, purely through which true facts are emphasized, which are omitted, and which images accompany the text.

docs.title: Diagram: Same Event, Two Frames
docs.text:
Same Event, Two Frames

Type: infographic

sim-id: same-event-two-frames Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Show two side-by-side, entirely factual headline-and-lead-paragraph pairs describing the same hypothetical event, differing only in framing choices, so students can see the framing effect operating without any factual falsehood present.

Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) — differentiate between factual content and framing choices in a news text. Bloom Verb: differentiate

Learning objective: Given two framings of the same factual event, students can identify the specific word choices, ordering, and visual choices producing the different impressions, without identifying either version as factually false.

Canvas layout: - Two side-by-side panels, each showing a headline, a one-paragraph lead, and a representative image placeholder - Below both panels, a highlighted-differences toggle

Interactive controls: - Toggle: "Highlight Word Choice Differences" — underlines the specific words that differ in emotional register between the two panels (e.g., "protesters" vs. "mob," "official" vs. "operative") - Click any highlighted word pair: infobox explains the connotation difference and cites this as the framing effect, not factual inaccuracy - Toggle: "Show Fact-Check" — a checkmark confirms both versions report the same underlying verifiable facts

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show both panels unhighlighted, prompting the student to spot differences on their own first Stage 2: On toggle, reveal highlighted word-choice differences Stage 3: On second toggle, confirm both are factually accurate, isolating framing as the sole variable

Instructional Rationale: An Analyze-level framing objective requires students to separate two things usually experienced together — factual content and framing choice. Presenting two factually verified panels side-by-side, with an explicit fact-check confirmation, is necessary because students otherwise default to treating "differently framed" as synonymous with "one side lying."

Implementation: p5.js or HTML/CSS panel layout with a JS toggle that applies/removes highlight spans on pre-marked text.

Recognizing headline bias and the framing effect requires media literacy: the set of skills needed to access, analyze, evaluate, and create media critically, including the ability to identify bias, verify claims, and recognize persuasive techniques. Media literacy is this chapter's central applied skill — everything that follows builds toward it.

docs.title: Bias in Fictional and Entertainment Media
docs.text:
Entertainment media has its own documented patterns of bias, distinct from but related to news framing. Stereotype in media refers to the recurring use of oversimplified, often inaccurate character traits assigned to a demographic group across many films, shows, or advertisements, reinforcing the general stereotype concept from Chapter 2 through sheer repetition. Repetition matters here: a single stereotyped character is a choice; a stereotype that recurs across hundreds of productions becomes a cultural pattern with its own name and its own measurable effect on audience assumptions.

Two specific, well-documented casting patterns extend this general pattern. Tokenized casting is the practice of including a single character from a marginalized group in an otherwise homogeneous cast, often in a minor or narrowly defined role, mirroring the tokenism concept from Chapter 2 in a specifically media context. Whitewashing is the practice of casting white actors in roles originally written for, or historically based on, people of color, or of altering a story's racial or ethnic context to center white characters. Whitewashing differs from tokenized casting in direction: tokenized casting includes a marginalized presence in a minimal way, while whitewashing actively replaces a marginalized presence that a story's own source material specified.

Here is a summary comparing the media-bias patterns this chapter has named so far:

Pattern What Happens Primary Media Type Colorism in media Favoring lighter skin tone within a group Casting, advertising, lighting Beauty standard bias Favoring one narrow standard of attractiveness Casting, advertising, editorial Headline bias Different word choice by group in news News Stereotype in media Repeated oversimplified traits assigned to a group Film, TV, advertising Tokenized casting One minor character representing a group Film, TV Whitewashing Replacing a group's story with white leads Film, TV

docs.title: Bias Beyond Human Editors: Digital and Algorithmic Media
docs.text:
Media bias is no longer produced only by human editors and casting directors. Digital media bias describes patterns of unequal representation, visibility, or moderation that emerge on digital and social media platforms — through what content gets promoted, demonetized, or removed — often without any single identifiable human decision-maker for a given case. Underneath much digital media bias sits algorithmic bias: systematic and repeatable errors in a computer system's output that create unfair outcomes for particular groups, arising from biased training data, biased design choices, or biased proxy measures, even when no individual programmer intended discrimination.

Algorithmic bias connects directly back to this chapter's earlier concepts — an algorithm trained on decades of stereotype-laden and whitewashed media content will tend to reproduce those same patterns at scale, faster and with less visible human accountability than a single editor's individual decision.

docs.title: Verifying and Responding to Bias
docs.text:
Faced with all of the patterns this chapter has named, a media-literate reader needs two more tools: a way to check claims, and a way to respond to distortion. Source validity — introduced in Chapter 1 in general terms, applied here specifically — is the degree to which a media source can be trusted based on its track record, methodology, transparency about sourcing, and independence from conflicts of interest. Checking source validity is how a media-literate reader distinguishes ordinary framing bias, which every outlet exhibits to some degree, from propaganda: media content deliberately designed to promote a particular political or ideological agenda through selective, exaggerated, or false information, rather than to inform.

The distinction matters because the appropriate response differs: ordinary framing bias calls for cross-referencing multiple sources (source corroboration, Chapter 1); propaganda calls for identifying and naming the deliberate distortion itself.

Beyond identifying bias, this course asks you to practice an active response: counter-storytelling, the deliberate practice of telling stories from marginalized perspectives to challenge dominant, stereotyped, or incomplete media narratives — the media-specific application of the counter-narrative concept introduced in Chapter 1. Counter-storytelling is not simply complaining about bias; it is the constructive half of media literacy, and it directly previews the capstone research project you will undertake in Chapter 14.

docs.title: Diagram: Media Literacy Checklist Sorter
docs.text:
Media Literacy Checklist Sorter

Type: microsim

sim-id: media-literacy-checklist-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Give students a repeatable diagnostic tool: presented with a short media excerpt, sort its features into "ordinary framing," "specific named bias pattern," or "likely propaganda."

Bloom Taxonomy: Evaluate (L5) — classify a media excerpt's features against defined criteria. Bloom Verb: classify

Learning objective: Given six short excerpt cards drawn from this chapter's named patterns (headline bias, stereotype in media, algorithmic bias, propaganda, and two neutral control examples), students can sort each card into the correct category and justify the sort using this chapter's vocabulary.

Canvas layout: - Top: a shuffled row of six excerpt cards (short text snippets, each illustrating one pattern from this chapter, clearly fictional/illustrative rather than pulled from a real current news source) - Bottom: three labeled drop zones — "Ordinary Framing," "Named Bias Pattern (specify which)," "Likely Propaganda"

Interactive controls: - Drag-and-drop each card into a drop zone - When dropping into "Named Bias Pattern," a dropdown appears requiring the student to specify which pattern (headline bias, stereotype in media, colorism in media, etc.) - "Check My Sorting" button reveals correct placements with a one-sentence justification for each

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Six shuffled cards, no feedback yet Stage 2: After each drop, card snaps into its zone (no correctness feedback yet, to allow full sorting first) Stage 3: On "Check My Sorting," each card is marked correct/incorrect with justification text shown

Instructional Rationale: An Evaluate-level classification objective requires learners to apply multiple criteria simultaneously, not recall one definition at a time. A sorting task with a delayed "check" step (rather than instant per-card feedback) forces students to apply the full chapter's vocabulary before receiving correctness signals, closer to how they'll need to evaluate real, un-labeled media independently.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with draggable card objects and defined drop-zone rectangles; a small local dataset of six illustrative excerpt cards with correct-category metadata.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Media representation is measurable through colorism in media and beauty standard bias in casting and advertising, and through headline bias and the framing effect in news.
  • Media literacy is the skill set needed to recognize these patterns; entertainment media adds its own patterns — stereotype in media, tokenized casting, and whitewashing.
  • Digital media bias and algorithmic bias show these patterns operating at platform scale, often without a single identifiable human decision-maker.
  • Checking source validity distinguishes ordinary bias from deliberate propaganda; counter-storytelling is the constructive response this course asks you to practice.

Chapter 9 deepens one thread introduced in Chapter 5 — tribal sovereignty — into its own full treatment of Indigenous history and contemporary voice.
