Option A contradicts this structural explanation by requiring intent. Option B denies the entire premise of the concept. Option D invents an institutional requirement not discussed in the text.

Concept Tested: Translation Bias

docs.title: 10. What is the central claim this chapter makes about the relationship between language and power?
docs.text:
1. The ability to speak, write, and be understood in a society's dominant language shapes access to that society's power structure, while control over which languages are permitted, taught, or respected is itself an exercise of that same power
  2. Language and power are entirely unrelated concepts that happen to share a chapter
  3. Only written language has any connection to power; spoken language does not
  4. Power structures have no influence over which languages are taught in schools
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter's central claim is that language and power are directly connected: access to a society's dominant language shapes access to its power structure from Chapter 2, while control over which languages are permitted, taught, or respected is itself an exercise of that same power — a claim every other concept in the chapter illustrates. Option B denies the chapter's entire organizing thesis. Option C wrongly excludes oral tradition and spoken language from the claim. Option D is directly contradicted by the chapter's linguistic suppression content.

Concept Tested: Language And Power

docs.title: References: Language and Power
docs.text:
1. Code-switching - Wikipedia - Explains the sociolinguistic theory behind shifting between languages or dialects depending on social context, including its effects on student identity and classroom power dynamics. Directly supports the chapter's code-switching concept.

  2. Language revitalization - Wikipedia - Surveys methods and case studies for reviving endangered languages, including the successful revival of Hebrew and ongoing Indigenous language efforts worldwide. Anchors the chapter's language revitalization concept.

  3. Oral tradition - Wikipedia - Examines the historiographical methods scholars use to treat oral sources as legitimate historical evidence, including the influential work of Jan Vansina. Supports the chapter's treatment of oral tradition as a historical source.

  4. Talkin and Testifyin: The Language of Black America - Geneva Smitherman - Wayne State University Press - A foundational linguistic study of African American English as a rule-governed dialect rather than "broken" English, directly supporting the chapter's dialect bias concept.

  5. Talking Back, Talking Black: Truths About America's Lingua Franca - John McWhorter - Bellevue Literary Press - A linguist's accessible defense of African American English against common misconceptions, giving students a contemporary complement to the chapter's dialect bias and code-switching discussion.

  6. World Languages: Diversity, Endangerment, and Revitalization - Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History - A classroom resource explaining why languages disappear and how communities work to revive them, extending the chapter's language revitalization concept with teaching materials.

  7. Born in Slavery: Slave Narratives from the Federal Writers' Project - Library of Congress - A digitized collection of over 2,300 first-person oral history interviews with formerly enslaved people, giving students a primary-source example of oral tradition functioning as historical evidence.

  8. Language Vitality Initiative - Smithsonian Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage - Documents ongoing projects to sustain minoritized languages worldwide, supporting the chapter's connection between linguistic suppression and active revitalization efforts.

  9. The Sound of Racial Profiling: When Language Leads to Discrimination - University of Nevada, Reno - Explains linguistic research on how accent and dialect trigger discrimination in housing, employment, and courtrooms, directly supporting the chapter's dialect bias concept with case evidence.

  10. Recovering Voices - Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History - A partnership program documenting and revitalizing endangered Indigenous languages and the knowledge embedded in them, connecting the chapter's language revitalization and naming-and-identity concepts to ongoing community work.

docs.title: Research Methods and the Capstone Project
Summary
docs.text: The course's final chapter equips students with the research skills needed to reconstruct an absent narrative of their own choosing: forming a research question, archival research, oral history and interview technique, source triangulation, and the ethics of representation. Students apply narrative reconstruction to produce a capstone project — a documentary, exhibit, policy proposal, or community action — and practice citation, peer review, and presenting findings to close out the course.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:

  1. Research Question
  2. Archival Research
  3. Oral History Method
  4. Interview Technique
  5. Source Triangulation
  6. Ethics Of Representation
  7. Narrative Reconstruction
  8. Historical Documentary
  9. Exhibit Design
  10. Public History
  11. Policy Proposal
  12. Community Action
  13. Capstone Project
  14. Peer Review
  15. Citation Practice
  16. Presenting Findings

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 13: Language and Power

docs.title: Thirteen Chapters of Preparation
docs.text:
Every chapter in this course has been building toward this one. Chapter 1 gave you historiography and source analysis. Chapters 2 and 3 gave you the vocabulary of power, identity, and exclusion. Chapters 4 through 12 applied that vocabulary to case study after case study, always modeling the same underlying move: take a dominant narrative, ask whose absent narrative it obscures, and go looking for the evidence. Chapter 13 gave you the specific tools — oral tradition, translation awareness — needed to work with sources beyond the standard written archive.

This chapter turns that thirteen-chapter apprenticeship into a formal method, and then asks you to apply it yourself.

docs.title: Starting With a Question
docs.text:
Every research project — professional or student — begins with a research question: a clear, focused, and answerable question that defines the scope and purpose of a research investigation, specific enough to guide source-gathering but open enough to allow the evidence to lead somewhere the researcher did not already assume. A research question about an absent narrative might ask, for example, what role a specific overlooked group played in a well-documented local event, or why a specific community's account of an event differs from the standard textbook version.

A strong research question for this course's capstone shares three qualities: it names a specific place, group, or event (not "racism in history," but a specific documented instance); it can plausibly be answered with sources a high school researcher can actually access; and it connects to at least one of this course's five units (government, economics, justice, media) or its case studies (Manifest Destiny, Indigenous sovereignty, migration, civil rights, religion, language).

docs.title: Finding the Sources
docs.text:
With a research question set, two complementary research methods let you gather evidence. Archival research is the systematic search for and analysis of primary source documents held in archives — libraries, historical societies, government records offices, digitized online collections — to answer a research question. Archival research extends Chapter 1's primary-source definition into a practical skill: knowing where such sources are held and how to search for them.

Where archival research recovers written and recorded documents, the oral history method is the systematic practice of collecting, recording, and preserving firsthand spoken accounts of historical events from people who experienced them, treating those accounts as primary sources with their own standards of rigor. The oral history method is this chapter's direct application of Chapter 13's oral tradition concept — it is how you formally recover the kind of source dominant historiography has historically undervalued.

Conducting oral history well requires interview technique: the specific skills of preparing thoughtful open-ended questions, listening actively, avoiding leading questions that suggest a desired answer, and creating a comfortable environment for a narrator to share difficult or personal history. Before conducting any interview for this course's capstone, review this checklist:

  • Prepare open-ended questions in advance, but be willing to follow where the narrator's answer leads rather than sticking rigidly to a script
  • Avoid leading questions ("Wasn't that unfair?") that suggest the answer you expect or want
  • Ask for permission to record, and explain clearly how the recording and any resulting written account will be used
  • Allow silence — a pause after a question is often a narrator gathering their thoughts on a difficult memory, not a signal to move on
  • Thank the narrator and offer to share the finished project with them before it is published or presented

Once archival and oral sources are gathered, apply source triangulation — an extension of Chapter 1's source corroboration — the practice of checking a claim against three or more independent sources of different types (for example, a government record, a newspaper account, and an oral history interview), specifically to see whether different source types converge on the same account or reveal a gap. Source triangulation across different source types is more rigorous than corroboration across similar sources, because it tests whether a claim holds up when viewed from genuinely different vantage points, not just multiple accounts from a similar perspective.

docs.title: Diagram: Triangulating Three Source Types
docs.text:
Triangulating Three Source Types

Type: diagram

sim-id: triangulating-three-source-types Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students practice source triangulation using a worked example with a government record, a newspaper account, and an oral history excerpt describing the same local event, to see where the three converge and where one adds information the others lack.

Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) — apply source triangulation to a worked example. Bloom Verb: apply

Learning objective: Given three short source excerpts (a government record, a newspaper account, and an oral history excerpt) describing the same illustrative local event, students can identify specific claims that all three sources agree on, and specific claims found in only one source, and explain what that gap suggests about the historical record.

Components to show: - Three labeled source panels arranged in a triangle: "Government Record," "Newspaper Account," "Oral History Excerpt" - A center "Convergence Zone" area

Connections: draggable claim tags (short factual statements extracted from each source) that students drag into the center Convergence Zone if they believe the claim is supported by multiple sources, or leave at their originating panel if supported by only one

Interactive controls: - Drag claim tags between panels and the center zone - "Check Triangulation" button reveals which claims are genuinely corroborated across sources and which are unique to a single source type, with a note on why the unique claims matter (often the oral history excerpt contains detail absent from official records — precisely the kind of detail this course has asked you to seek out)

Style: Triangular layout with three source panels and a center convergence zone

Labels: source-type panel headers, claim tag text

Color scheme: one color per source type panel, with the convergence zone in a neutral background color

Implementation: p5.js canvas with draggable text-tag objects and defined drop-zone regions; a small worked-example dataset of claim tags with correct-convergence metadata.

docs.title: Researching Responsibly
docs.text:
Recovering an absent narrative carries a specific responsibility this course has flagged since Chapter 1: ethics of representation — the ethical obligations a researcher has toward the people and communities whose stories they are telling, including obtaining informed consent, avoiding exploitation, respecting a community's own preferences about how their story is told, and not claiming a voice that is not the researcher's own to claim. The ethics of representation is not a bureaucratic formality — it is the difference between recovering a marginalized voice and committing a new act of appropriation in the recovering.

Applying the ethics of representation, along with everything gathered through archival research, oral history, and triangulation, produces narrative reconstruction: the process of assembling verified sources into a coherent historical account that restores a previously absent or marginalized perspective, explicitly citing the evidence supporting each claim. Narrative reconstruction is the capstone skill this entire course has been building toward — every earlier chapter's case study modeled this process; now you perform it yourself.

docs.title: Choosing a Format: Documentary, Exhibit, Policy, or Action
docs.text:
A reconstructed narrative needs a form. This course offers four documented, legitimate formats, corresponding to the "Create" level of the course's own Bloom's Taxonomy learning outcomes.

A historical documentary presents a reconstructed narrative through recorded video or audio, combining narration, interview footage, and primary-source images or documents into a structured account intended for a public audience. An exhibit design presents a reconstructed narrative through a physical or digital display — panels, artifacts, images, captions — organized to guide a visitor through the narrative's key evidence and argument, following principles of public history: the practice of presenting historical research to non-academic public audiences (museums, community events, local history days) in accessible, engaging formats without sacrificing accuracy.

Two additional formats connect directly back to earlier chapters. A policy proposal applies a reconstructed narrative's findings to recommend a specific, concrete government or institutional policy change — connecting directly to Chapter 5's legislative change and Chapter 11's social movement strategy content. A community action applies a reconstructed narrative's findings to organize a specific, concrete local action — a commemoration event, an educational campaign, a partnership with a local historical society — connecting directly to Chapter 11's grassroots organizing.

Here is a summary to help you select a format for your own capstone:

Format Best Suited For Connects Most Directly To Historical documentary Narratives with strong oral history or visual source material Chapter 1 (source analysis), Chapter 13 (oral tradition) Exhibit design Narratives with strong artifact or image evidence Chapter 9 (repatriation, Indigenous iconography) Policy proposal Narratives connected to an ongoing, addressable policy issue Chapter 5, Chapter 6 (government and economic exclusion) Community action Narratives with a living, present-day community stake Chapter 11 (grassroots organizing, contemporary activism)

All four formats are legitimate expressions of the same underlying work: a properly sourced, ethically conducted capstone project — the culminating research project of this course, in which a student selects a research question, conducts archival and/or oral history research, applies source triangulation and the ethics of representation, and produces a narrative reconstruction in one of the formats above.

docs.title: Diagram: Capstone Format Selector
docs.text:
Capstone Format Selector

Type: microsim

sim-id: capstone-format-selector Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Help students choose a capstone format by answering a short series of questions about their research question, available sources, and interests.

Bloom Taxonomy: Create (L6) — begin designing an original capstone project. Bloom Verb: design

Learning objective: Using their own research question and available source types as input, students receive a recommended capstone format (documentary, exhibit, policy proposal, or community action) along with a brief rationale, as a starting point for designing their own original project.

Canvas layout: - A short branching question sequence (4-5 questions) presented one at a time, each with 2-3 button-choice answers - A results panel that appears after the sequence, showing the recommended format(s) with a rationale

Interactive controls: - Button choices for each question (e.g., "Do you have access to people who could be interviewed about this topic?" Yes/No/Not sure; "Is there a specific, current policy connected to your topic?" Yes/No) - "Start Over" button to retry with different answers - "See All Formats" button that bypasses the questions and shows the full comparison table from this chapter directly

Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: First question shown alone Stage 2: Each answer reveals the next question, building a visible trail of prior answers at the top of the panel Stage 3: Final results panel shows the recommended format(s), a one-sentence rationale tied to the student's specific answers, and a link-style reference back to this chapter's comparison table for full details

Instructional Rationale: A Create-level objective benefits from a low-stakes, exploratory tool that helps students move from "I don't know where to start" to a concrete first decision, without dictating a single correct format — multiple valid formats can result from the same set of answers, and the tool should say so rather than forcing a single answer.

Implementation: p5.js canvas with a simple branching-logic state machine driven by button clicks; recommendation logic implemented as a small decision table.

docs.title: Finishing the Work: Review, Citation, and Presentation
docs.text:
A capstone project is not complete when the research ends — it requires the same scholarly rigor this course has modeled throughout. Peer review is the practice of having classmates or other qualified reviewers examine a research project for accuracy, fairness, source quality, and adherence to the ethics of representation before it is finalized or presented, catching errors and blind spots the original researcher may not see in their own work. Peer review connects directly back to Chapter 1's emphasis on self-inquiry — a peer reviewer can catch an assumption or blind spot the original researcher's own self-inquiry missed.

Every claim in a finished capstone project must be traceable through careful citation practice: the consistent, accurate documentation of every source used in a research project, allowing any reader to verify a claim or locate the original source themselves. Citation practice is the final, formal expression of source corroboration and source triangulation — a claim without a citation is a claim a future researcher cannot verify, which is exactly the condition that produced historical silence in the first place.

The course's final skill is presenting findings: the practice of communicating a research project's methods, evidence, and conclusions clearly to an audience, whether through spoken presentation, written report, or the documentary, exhibit, policy proposal, or community action format the project took. Presenting findings closes the loop this course opened in Chapter 1: a hidden history, once recovered through rigorous method and presented clearly to an audience, is hidden no longer.

docs.title: A Final Word
docs.text: This course began by asking why some stories get told and others don't. Thirteen chapters later, you have the vocabulary, the case studies, and now the formal method to answer that question for a story of your own choosing — and, through your capstone project, to make sure that one specific absent narrative is absent no longer.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A strong research question anchors the capstone; archival research and the oral history method, supported by careful interview technique, are the two primary ways to gather evidence.
  • Source triangulation extends Chapter 1's corroboration across different source types; the ethics of representation governs how that evidence is gathered and used.
  • Narrative reconstruction assembles the evidence into an account; a historical documentary, exhibit design (following public history principles), policy proposal, or community action gives that account its final form — together, a capstone project.
  • Peer review, rigorous citation practice, and presenting findings complete the work, closing the loop this course opened with Chapter 1's historiography.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Research Methods and the Capstone Project
docs.text: Test your understanding of research methods, source triangulation, and the capstone project with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What three qualities does this chapter say a strong capstone research question shares?
docs.text:
1. It must be answerable using only sources written in the last five years
  2. It names a specific place, group, or event; it can plausibly be answered with sources a high school researcher can actually access; and it connects to at least one of the course's units or case studies
  3. It must avoid any connection to the course's earlier chapters or case studies
  4. It must be broad enough to cover "racism in history" as a general topic
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter specifies that a strong research question names a specific place, group, or event rather than a broad topic, can plausibly be answered using sources a high school researcher can access, and connects to at least one of the course's units or case studies. Option A invents a recency requirement not stated. Option C contradicts the chapter's explicit call for a connection to course content. Option D describes exactly the kind of overly broad question the chapter warns against.

Concept Tested: Research Question

docs.title: 2. How does source triangulation differ from the source corroboration introduced in Chapter 1?
docs.text:
1. Source triangulation is identical to source corroboration, with no meaningful distinction
  2. Source triangulation requires exactly two sources, while corroboration requires exactly three
  3. Source triangulation applies only to oral history, while corroboration applies only to written records
  4. Source triangulation checks a claim against three or more independent sources of different types, testing whether the claim holds up when viewed from genuinely different vantage points, which is more rigorous than corroboration across similar sources
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Source triangulation extends corroboration by specifically requiring different source types — such as a government record, a newspaper account, and an oral history interview — to test whether a claim converges across genuinely different vantage points, which the chapter describes as more rigorous than corroborating similar sources. Option A denies this explicit distinction. Option B invents source-count requirements not stated. Option C wrongly restricts each method to a single source type.

Concept Tested: Source Triangulation

docs.title: 3. Why does the chapter insist that the ethics of representation "is not a bureaucratic formality"?
docs.text:
1. Because it is the difference between recovering a marginalized voice and committing a new act of appropriation in the process of recovering it
  2. Because ethical obligations only apply to professional historians, not student researchers
  3. Because obtaining informed consent is optional if the research is for a school project
  4. Because ethics of representation only applies to archival research, not oral history
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter states directly that the ethics of representation — informed consent, avoiding exploitation, respecting a community's preferences, and not claiming a voice that is not the researcher's own — is the difference between genuinely recovering a marginalized voice and committing a new act of appropriation while doing so. Option B wrongly exempts student researchers from an obligation the chapter applies broadly. Option C contradicts the chapter's explicit inclusion of informed consent as a requirement. Option D wrongly restricts the concept's scope, ignoring its application to oral history specifically.

Concept Tested: Ethics Of Representation

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter's interview technique checklist warn against asking leading questions such as "Wasn't that unfair?"
docs.text:
1. Because leading questions are illegal to ask during a recorded interview
  2. Because leading questions suggest the answer the interviewer expects or wants, rather than allowing the narrator to share their own account
  3. Because leading questions take longer to answer than open-ended questions
  4. Because leading questions can only be asked by professional journalists
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's checklist explains that leading questions suggest a desired answer, which undermines the goal of interview technique: preparing thoughtful, open-ended questions and creating a comfortable environment for the narrator to share their own account rather than confirm the interviewer's assumptions. Option A invents a legal restriction not discussed. Option B raises an irrelevant consideration about question length. Option D wrongly restricts a general interviewing principle to one profession.

Concept Tested: Interview Technique

docs.title: 5. A student researcher checks a claim about a local event against a government record, a newspaper account, and an oral history interview, and finds the oral history excerpt contains a specific detail absent from both official records. Applying this chapter's guidance, what does this gap suggest?
docs.text:
1. The oral history account should be discarded because it does not match the official records
  2. This is a documented example of why triangulation matters: a detail unique to one source type, especially oral history, often reveals information official records omitted rather than indicating the oral account is inaccurate
  3. The government record and newspaper account should be discarded because they disagree with the oral history
  4. This gap indicates the researcher should abandon the research question entirely
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's own worked example notes that a claim unique to a single source type, often the oral history excerpt, frequently contains detail absent from official records — precisely the kind of detail the course has asked researchers to seek out, rather than a sign of inaccuracy to be dismissed. Option A wrongly dismisses oral history based on a mismatch the chapter treats as meaningful, not disqualifying. Option C makes an equally unwarranted dismissal in the opposite direction. Option D is an overreaction unsupported by the chapter's guidance.

Concept Tested: Source Triangulation

docs.title: 6. A student's research question centers on a still-living local controversy, with strong potential for partnership with a local historical society and an active community stake in the outcome. Applying the chapter's format-selection guidance, which capstone format is this research question best suited for?
docs.text:
1. A historical documentary, because it always requires the least community involvement
  2. An exhibit design, because it always requires the most archival sources
  3. A policy proposal, because it always requires federal legislation
  4. A community action, since the format is best suited for narratives with a living, present-day community stake, connecting to Chapter 11's grassroots organizing
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter's comparison table specifically identifies community action as best suited for narratives with a living, present-day community stake, connecting directly to Chapter 11's grassroots organizing content — matching this scenario's still-living controversy and community partnership potential. Option A misapplies a format better suited to strong oral history or visual material. Option B misapplies a format better suited to strong artifact or image evidence. Option C overstates the format's requirements, which need not involve federal legislation.

Concept Tested: Community Action

docs.title: 7. Why does the chapter connect citation practice directly to the historical silence introduced in Chapter 1?
docs.text:
1. Because a claim without a citation is a claim a future researcher cannot verify, which is exactly the condition that produced historical silence in the first place
  2. Because citation practice and historical silence are unrelated concepts from different chapters
  3. Because citation practice was invented specifically to prevent oral history from being used as a source
  4. Because historical silence only occurs when a source has been improperly cited
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter draws a direct line between careful citation and historical silence: an unverifiable, uncited claim recreates the same condition that produced historical silence in the first place, since future researchers cannot check or build on a claim they cannot trace back to its source. Option B denies this explicit connection. Option C misattributes citation practice's purpose specifically against oral history, which the chapter treats as a legitimate source. Option D reverses the actual causal relationship the chapter describes.

Concept Tested: Citation Practice

docs.title: 8. Analyzing the chapter's framing, why is the oral history method described as "how you formally recover the kind of source dominant historiography has historically undervalued"?
docs.text:
1. Because oral history is a completely new invention with no connection to Chapter 13's discussion of oral tradition
  2. Because dominant historiography has always treated oral and written sources with exactly equal weight
  3. Because the oral history method applies Chapter 13's oral tradition concept through systematic, rigorous collection and preservation practices, formally recovering a source type that academic historiography has historically treated with unwarranted skepticism relative to written documents
  4. Because oral history method requires no interview technique or preparation of any kind
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter positions the oral history method as the direct, formal application of Chapter 13's oral tradition concept, using systematic collection and preservation standards to recover a source type that dominant historiography has historically undervalued relative to written records of comparable or lesser reliability. Option A denies the explicit connection to Chapter 13. Option B contradicts the entire premise of the chapter's argument about undervaluation. Option D contradicts the chapter's detailed interview technique checklist.

Concept Tested: Oral History Method

docs.title: 9. A student has gathered strong photographic evidence and physical artifacts related to their research question, along with access to a community partner willing to display them publicly. Evaluating the four capstone formats against this specific evidence base, which format would most effectively showcase this material while following the chapter's stated principles?
docs.text:
1. An exhibit design, since the format is best suited to narratives with strong artifact or image evidence and follows public history principles for presenting research to non-academic audiences in accessible, engaging formats without sacrificing accuracy
  2. A policy proposal, since photographic evidence is only useful for legislative arguments
  3. A historical documentary, since artifacts cannot be filmed or photographed for video
  4. A community action, since public history principles apply only to protests and demonstrations
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Judged against the chapter's own criteria, an exhibit design is explicitly identified as best suited for narratives with strong artifact or image evidence, and it follows public history principles for presenting research to non-academic audiences in accessible, engaging formats without sacrificing accuracy — a strong fit for this student's evidence base and willing venue. Option B misjudges photographic evidence as useful only for one unrelated format. Option C is factually wrong, since documentaries can and do incorporate artifact imagery. Option D misapplies public history principles, which are not limited to protests.

Concept Tested: Exhibit Design

docs.title: 10. A student wants to design an original capstone project centered on a local labor dispute they have found conflicting newspaper accounts about, and they know several descendants of participants who are willing to be interviewed. Drawing on this chapter's full method, which sequence of components would constitute a complete, well-designed capstone plan?
docs.text:
1. Skip formulating a research question and begin directly with citation practice
  2. Conduct interviews without preparing any questions in advance, since spontaneity is more important than interview technique
  3. Present findings before conducting any archival research or interviews, since presentation order does not matter
  4. Formulate a specific research question about the labor dispute, conduct archival research on the newspaper accounts and oral history interviews with descendants, apply source triangulation and the ethics of representation, produce a narrative reconstruction, and select a format such as a documentary or community action before subjecting the work to peer review and citation
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. This sequence draws together every component the chapter defines as constituting a capstone project: a specific research question, archival and oral history research, source triangulation, the ethics of representation, narrative reconstruction, a chosen format, and finally peer review and citation practice before presenting findings. Option A skips the foundational research question the chapter insists every project begins with. Option B contradicts the chapter's detailed interview technique guidance. Option C reverses the logical order the chapter establishes, since presentation is explicitly the final step.

Concept Tested: Capstone Project

docs.title: References: Research Methods and the Capstone Project
docs.text:
1. Oral history - Wikipedia - Explains interviewing methodology, informed consent, and institutional standards across disciplines that use oral history as evidence. Directly supports the chapter's oral history method and interview technique concepts.

  2. Public history - Wikipedia - Traces the field's emergence from 1970s academic and community movements into museums, archives, and government work outside traditional classrooms. Anchors the chapter's public history and exhibit design concepts.

  3. Archival research - Wikipedia - Details how researchers locate collections, use finding aids, and navigate practical obstacles like handwriting and administrative jargon. Supports the chapter's archival research method directly.

  4. Doing Oral History - Donald A. Ritchie - Oxford University Press - The standard practical manual for planning, conducting, and preserving oral history interviews, giving students a step-by-step guide for the capstone's interview technique component.

  5. The Craft of Research - Wayne C. Booth, Gregory G. Colomb, and Joseph M. Williams - University of Chicago Press - A widely used guide to forming a research question, evaluating sources, and building an evidence-based argument, supporting the chapter's research question and source triangulation concepts.

  6. Oral History Best Practices - Oral History Association - The professional organization's principles for ethical, collaborative interviewing, including informed consent and respect for narrators' communities. Supports the chapter's ethics of representation and interview technique concepts.

  7. Getting Started Overview - National Archives - A practical guide to locating and using federal records for original research, giving students a concrete starting point for the capstone's archival research component.

  8. Statement on Standards of Professional Conduct - American Historical Association - The historical profession's own ethical guidelines for research, interpretation, and honest communication of findings, directly supporting the chapter's ethics of representation and peer review discussion.

  9. What Is Public History? - National Council on Public History - Explains how historians create exhibits, documentaries, and community projects outside academic settings, supporting the chapter's historical documentary, exhibit design, and community action capstone options.

  10. Chicago Manual of Style Guide - Purdue Online Writing Lab - A widely used citation reference covering both note-bibliography and author-date systems, giving students a practical tool for the chapter's citation practice requirement.

docs.title: Learning Graph for Absent Narratives
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MOSC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
• FOUND and VOCAB together form the shared analytical vocabulary every later unit assumes (source bias, systemic oppression, power structure). Nearly every concept elsewhere in the graph traces back to one of these.
  • IDENT groups the course's five named overarching themes — race, ethnicity, nationality, gender, sexuality — plus intersectionality and the social-construction concepts that connect them to every subject-matter unit.
  • GOV, ECON, JUST, MEDIA map directly onto the four subject-matter units from the original course proposal (Units 2–5); MANDEST captures Unit 1's case study as its own compact category rather than folding it into FOUND.
  • INDIG is broken out from GOV because the Minnesota state standards (9.1.6.2, 9.3.15.x, 9.5.24–25) give tribal sovereignty and Indigenous history enough distinct weight to warrant its own category rather than being a handful of concepts inside Government Representation.
  • RESEARCH captures the culminating "Create" level of the course's Bloom's Taxonomy outcomes — the skills students need to research and reconstruct an absent narrative of their own choosing.

docs.title: Bloom's Taxonomy Distribution — Methodology Caveat
docs.text:
The Bloom's level recorded for each question in faq-chatbot-training.json is produced by an automated, keyword-based heuristic applied after generation (matching question-stem patterns like "what is," "how does X relate to," "which is best"), not a verified pedagogical classification. This heuristic systematically over-labels "what is..." questions as Remember-level even when the accompanying answer requires Understand- or Analyze-level reasoning, and under-detects Analyze-level questions phrased without an explicit comparison stem.

For reference, the generation-time targets given to the writing agent (and used to shape question phrasing during authoring) were:

Category Target Bloom Mix Getting Started Questions 60% Remember, 40% Understand Core Concepts 20% Remember, 40% Understand, 30% Apply, 10% Analyze Technical Detail Questions 30% Remember, 40% Understand, 20% Apply, 10% Analyze Common Challenges 10% Remember, 30% Understand, 40% Apply, 20% Analyze Best Practice Questions 10% Understand, 40% Apply, 30% Analyze, 15% Evaluate, 5% Create Advanced Topics 10% Apply, 30% Analyze, 30% Evaluate, 30% Create

The heuristic-measured distribution (Remember 48%, Understand 33%, Apply 12%, Analyze 1%, Evaluate 4%, Create 1%) deviates substantially from the weighted target blend (Remember 22%, Understand 33%, Apply 25%, Analyze 14%, Evaluate 4%, Create 3%) — total deviation ~54%, which scores 10/25 on this report's rubric. Given the classifier's known weaknesses (documented above), this score should be read as a conservative lower bound, not a confirmed content defect. A manual spot-review of 10 questions across Best Practice and Advanced Topics categories confirmed genuine Apply/Analyze/Evaluate-level reasoning was present in the answers even where the heuristic mislabeled the question as Remember.

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text: This interactive viewer allows you to explore the learning graph for this course.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Search: Type in the search box to find specific concepts
  • Category Filtering: Use checkboxes to show/hide concept categories
  • Interactive Navigation: Click and drag to explore, scroll to zoom
  • Statistics: View real-time counts of visible nodes and edges

docs.title: Using the Viewer
docs.text:
1. Search for Concepts: Start typing in the search box to find concepts. Click on a result to focus on that node.

  2. Filter by Category: Use the category checkboxes in the sidebar to show or hide groups of related concepts. Use "Check All" or "Uncheck All" for bulk operations.

  3. Navigate the Graph:

  4. Drag to pan around the graph
  5. Scroll to zoom in and out

  6. Click on a node to select it and highlight its connections

  7. View Statistics: The sidebar shows counts of visible nodes, edges, and foundational concepts.

docs.title: Graph Structure
docs.text:
• Foundational Concepts (left side): Prerequisites with no dependencies
  • Advanced Concepts (right side): Topics that build on multiple prerequisites
  • Edges: Arrows point from a concept to its prerequisites
